paragraphs.text: Commentary § 3.15:1 Rule 3.15 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.15. 1. Rule applies to municipal bylaws In Okotoks (Town) v. Foothills (Municipal District) No. 31, 2013 ABCA 222, the Court said, at paragraph 9: 9 … First, Okotoks submits that the enactment of a bylaw is not a “decision or act” of a body; hence Rule 3.15(2) does not apply. In our view, the Rule should not be read so narrowly. A municipal council can only act by resolution or bylaw: MGA section 180. Accordingly, we conclude that a bylaw is a decision or act of the municipality subject to the remedies in Rules 3.15(1)(a) and (b). In so holding, mindful of the nature of those remedies, we are not to be taken to have suggested that there exists some wide-ranging power to review the substance of bylaws for “reasonableness”. 2. Domestic tribunals In Falk v. Calgary Real Estate Board Co-Operative Ltd., 2000 ABQB 296, 2000 CarswellAlta 428, 265 A.R. 60, 82 Alta. L.R. (3d) 201, the plaintiff was “subject to the Board's tribunals by virtue of the voluntary contractual relationship between herself and the Board. Therefore, the Board's disciplinary tribunals are of a private or domestic nature” (p. 65). On the question of whether the judicial review provisions in the Rules of Court apply to consensual (domestic) tribunals, Rowbotham, J. said, at p. 66: I find that although the Board's disciplinary tribunals are domestic, their decisions are subject to judicial review for the limited purposes discussed in [Kaplan v. Canadian Institute of Actuaries (1994), 161 A.R. 321 (Q.B.); affirmed (1997), 206 A.R. 268 (C.A.); additional reasons at (1998), 212 A.R. 376, 168 W.A.C. 376, 60 Alta. L.R. (3d) 251 (C.A.); leave to appeal refused (1998), 227 N.R. 89 (note), 219 A.R. 160, 179 W.A.C. 160 (S.C.C.)]. The court is entitled to review the decisions to determine whether the tribunals have acted within their jurisdiciton; to ensure that decisions within their jurisdiction are not patently unreasonable; and to prevent breaches of natural justice or fairness. In Homestead Housing Co-operative Ltd. v. Barth, 2016 ABQB 538, 2016 CarswellAlta 1916 (Master), Master Schlosser said: 26 Can a private organization be judicially reviewed? Manderscheid J, in Slovenian Canadian (at para 29), after a review of authority, tells us that the Court can conduct a limited judicial review to determine whether (in that case) the Association violated its by-laws. In Lee v Yeung, Macklin J said (paras 29–31): 29 Despite the historical distinction between public and private law remedies, the courts have interpreted the Rules of Court as giving teeth to the declaratory remedy in the private law context. In Kaplan v Canadian Institute of Actuaries, 161 AR 321, [1994] A.J. No 868 (QB), Hunt J stated: 44 It seems to me that even if certiorari will not lie against a consensual tribunal, the court possesses broad enough powers under Rule 753.05 to grant the remedy it considers appropriate to the particular case, including the setting aside of an invalid decision or action … 30 In Falk v Calgary Real Estate Board Co-operative Ltd, 2000 ABQB 296, 265 AR 60, Rowbotham J considered Hunt J's reasoning in Kaplan and concluded: 13 I find that although the Board's disciplinary tribunals are domestic, their decisions are subject to judicial review for the limited purposes discussed in Kaplan, supra. The court is entitled to review the decisions to determine whether the tribunals have acted within their jurisdiction; to ensure that decisions within their jurisdiction are not patently unreasonable; and to prevent breaches of natural justice or fairness. In this case the decisions in question were within both tribunals' jurisdictions. Therefore, the substantive issue is whether these decisions should be set aside as being patently unreasonable; and to prevent breaches of natural justice or fairness …[Emphasis added] 31 Accordingly it appears that while, historically, judicial review was only available as a public law remedy, Knox does confirm that private bodies are prima facie only subject to private law remedies. Kaplan and Falk emphasize that judicial review is available in relation to decisions of private bodies for limited purposes. And now see: Wall v Judicial Committee of the Highwood Congregation of Jehovah's Witnesses (Wakeling JA, dissenting). 27 These cases leave no doubt that a limited judicial review of the decision of this private organization is available. 3. Service of application In Sedgwick v. Edmonton Real Estate Board Co-Operative Listing Bureau Limited, 2021 ABQB 59, 2021 CarswellAlta 121, affirmed 2022 ABCA 264, Justice Mandziuk found that service had not been effected as required by Rule 3.15(3)(b), and said: [39] There is no evidence before me that this notice was given. That would seem to represent a full stop to the application for judicial review (at least at this point). This is consistent with Graesser, J's decision in Peter Lehmann Wines Ltd v Vintage West Wine Marketing Inc, 2015 ABQB 481: lack of service on the Crown precluded a mandamus remedy “[b]ecause a Crown or statutory body is always implicated in administrative law, Rule 3.15(3)(b) … requires the Minister of Justice and Solicitor General for Alberta to be given notice of applications which ask the Court to contemplate any of the prerogative writs used to initiate a judicial review” (at para 47). [40] The relief sought here is prerogative in nature insofar as it arises from the judicial review argument. Therefore, the notice must be given. In ENMAX Corporation v. Alberta (Labour Relations Board), 2018 ABQB 431, 2018 CarswellAlta 1089, ENMAX filed an application (“the application”) for judicial review of a decision of the Alberta Labour Relations Board. ENMAX did not serve notice of the application upon the Association of Professional Engineers and Geoscientists of Alberta (APEGA) which had successfully obtained intervenor status in the application before the Board. Unions which had been served with notice of the application sought to have the application dismissed on the basis that APEGA had not been served. APEGA (which had received a “courtesy copy” of the application) had decided not to participate in the application; the Unions were relying on a deficiency about which APEGA did not care. Justice Hunt McDonald concluded that the obligation to serve notice of the application on APEGA as a “body directly affected by the application” was mandatory and could not be waived. Her Ladyship summarily dismissed ENMAX's application for judicial review, and said: 15 ENMAX claims that the Unions are trying to take unfair advantage of an alleged service irregularity, and highlights the fact that APEGA and the EITs are not the complaining parties. ENMAX states, “That a party did not receive a copy of the claim or received it by means other than those described in Part 11 of the Alberta Rules of Court is not determinative.” ENMAX argues that APEGA and the EITs had knowledge of the general nature of the ENMAX Application within the six-month limitation period, and this knowledge is sufficient to satisfy the policy reasons and purpose of the Rules. 16 ENMAX claims that to interpret rule 3.15 to require formal service on APEGA and the EITs leads to an absurd result because it frustrates the purpose of the Rules and leads to an unfair or unreasonable result. ENMAX states that formal service would not have altered the interest or participation level of APEGA or the EITs. 17 The object of service is a relevant consideration: Condominium Plan 9812082 v Battistella Developments Inc, 2014 ABQB 644 at para 11. However, I disagree with the assertion by ENMAX that establishing notice of an application for judicial review is sufficient. 18 An applicant has an obligation to follow legislated procedure: Raczynska v Alberta (Human Rights Commission), 2015 ABQB 494 at para 63. Rule 3.15(3) states that an originating application for judicial review must be served on every person or body directly affected by the application. This is a mandatory requirement. Rule 3.15 does not allow for discretion and does not differentiate between affected parties that oppose or support an application. 19 Knowledge of an application is not equivalent to service, even if there is knowledge of the general nature of the application. Furthermore, this court has previously found that a courtesy copy of an originating application does not equate to service: Lynne M Miller v Chief of the Commission and Tribunals, Alberta Human Rights Commission and The Workers' Compensation Board (27 January 2015), Calgary, 1401 045218 (ABQB). 20 In Raczynska, Justice Graesser acknowledged that the strict application of rule 3.15 may be viewed as harsh: at para 76. In Zimmer-Worker Estate v Alberta (Appeals Commission for Alberta Workers' Compensation) (7 October 2015), Edmonton, 1403-00907 (ABQB), Justice Simpson agreed at paragraph 28: […] this Court has no jurisdiction to provide relief by way of extending the Applicant time for naming and serving under the Workers Compensation Act or the Alberta Rules of Court. I agree with Graesser J's comment in Raczynska that this is a harsh position. However, until the legislature amends the legislation or our Court of Appeal provides authority to this Court by reference to the Judicature Act or otherwise it is not open for this Court to apply the Judicature Act and provide any relief regarding the requirements in the statue or the rules. 21 The fact that APEGA and the EITs had knowledge of the general nature of the ENMAX Application does not satisfy the mandatory service requirement in rule 3.15(3). Whether or not formal service would have altered the interest or participation level of APEGA or the EITs is irrelevant. This strict interpretation of the Rules may seem harsh but that does not mean the result is absurd or unreasonable. Can a party directly affected by an application waive the service obligation in rule 3.15? 22 Counsel for APEGA informed counsel for ENMAX that APEGA is interested in the outcome of the judicial review but is not interested in participating. Mr. Chai, spokesperson for the EITs, confirmed that the EITs are not interested in participating in the ENMAX Application since the position of the EITs aligns with and is represented by ENMAX. 23 ENMAX argues that benefitting parties may waive the benefits of a statute and that the intention to waive a right may be expressed in an informal fashion or inferred from conduct. ENMAX claims that by their advice and actions, APEGA and the EITs unilaterally and unequivocally waived the service requirement and the limitation period of rule 3.15. The Unions argue that APEGA and the EITs may waive their right to participate in the ENMAX Application but they cannot waive the applicant's mandatory service obligations. 24 In MacDonald v Royal Trust Corporation of Canada (1984), 54 AR 116 (ABQB) [MacDonald], Justice Brennan stated the general rule of waiver at para 12: It has long been established, that generally speaking, a person may waive the benefits of a statute unless to do so would be contrary to public policy; and such waiver is not contrary to public policy where the rights, privileges or advantages conferred by the statute are for the benefit of the individual in his private capacity as opposed to being for the benefit of the public as a whole. [citations omitted] 25 The applicants in the case were seeking a declaration pursuant to section 10(1) of the Interest Act, RSC c I-18, regarding the prepayment of a mortgage. The applicants had signed a contract renewing the mortgage; the contract was found to waive the beneficial prepayment provisions of the Interest Act. 26 In Heikkila v Alberta (Workers' Compensation Board, Appeals Commission), 2003 ABQB 544, Justice Hawco considered whether the respondents had waived the limitation defence. He decided the facts of the case did not establish that either of the respondents waived the limitation period of former rule 753. He did not discuss whether the respondents could have waived the applicant's service obligation. 27 In U(J) v Alberta (Director of Child Welfare), 2001 ABCA 125, the applicant failed to file a copy of the notice of appeal in the Provincial Court as was required under the Child Welfare Act, SA 1984, c C-8.1. The applicant asked the chambers judge to exercise parens patria jurisdiction to allow the appeal to proceed despite her non-compliance with the filing requirement. The Court of Appeal stated that the court does not have the jurisdiction to waive a statutory limitation period or a statutory filing requirement: at para 6. The Court of Appeal also said that the absence of a provision to allow the waiver of a statutory requirement does not mean there is a gap in the legislation: “if it was intended that such requirements could be overridden, the mandatory aspect of the legislation would be superfluous”: at para 7. 28 In MacDonald the general rule regarding waiver was found to apply to a prepayment rule that a mortgagor may be able to benefit from. In contrast, rule 3.15 imposes a mandatory obligation on the applicant. As with the filing requirement in U(J) and the limitation period in Heikkila, the service requirement in rule 3.15 is substantive in nature. 29 Rule 3.15 does not address waiver and I am not aware of a case that specifically considers whether a party directly affected by an application for judicial review may waive the applicant's service obligation. Considering the above cases and the strict interpretation of rule 3.15 previously noted, I agree with the Unions; APEGA and the EITs may waive their right to participate in the proceedings but they cannot waive ENMAX's mandatory service obligations. In Kyambadde v. Calgary Police Service, 2024 ABKB 370, the Minister of Justice was not served with the originating application for judicial review. It was another person directly affected by the judicial review application who raised the issue. Justice Poelman said: [13] One might be sympathetic with the Minister not being served. Even now, the Minister declines to be involved. How the Minister responds, however, is not determinative. A Crown or statutory body always is implicated in administrative law and thus must be given notice of applications that ask the court to contemplate a judicial review; an order cannot be granted without such notice: Peter Lehmann Wines Ltd v Vintage West Wine Marketing Inc, 2015 ABQB 481 at paras 47 and 48; ENMAX Corporation v Alberta (Labour Relations Board), 2018 ABQB 431 at para 29. 4. Service of notice of the application suspends proceedings in the Alberta Court of Justice In R. v. Hosack (1988), 85 A.R. 98 (Q.B.), Justice Cooke said that if an application is made in the Court of King's Bench for judicial review of a decision made by a judge of the Provincial Court of Alberta (now a Justice of the Alberta Court of Justice), then upon service of notice of the application on the Court of Justice, that Court's jurisdiction to act in the matter is suspended. His Lordship said: [18] The Supreme Court of Canada in the case of R. v. Batchelor (1977), 1978 CanLII 35 (SCC), 18 N.R. 416; 38 C.C.C. 2d) 113, makes it clear that the lower Court's jurisdiction to act is dormant from the time of service of the writ as opposed to the time of the return to the writ. Laskin, C.J.C., at 128 C.C.C. states: “It seems to me that, however the matter is regarded, there must be a suspension of jurisdiction when an application to quash or a combined application to prohibit and to quash is served on the inferior Court with the command, under the Rules, to make a return forthwith. The Judge, compelled to make the return, cannot, unless he risks disobedience with its attendant consequences, go on with the matter before him until the application to the superior Court is disposed of by dismissal thereof. … [30] At page 128 of the Batchelor case, Laskin, C.J.C., states: “As put by Letourneau, The Prerogative Writs in Canadian Criminal Law and Procedure (1976), at p. 161: ‘… in criminal law, the transmission the record of the proceedings of the superior court, as required to be made forthwith by most rules of court on an application for certiorari, in fact operates as a stay of proceedings. “The author goes on to say that the inferior court is deprived of its jurisdiction to resume the proceedings as, after the removal, nothing is left before it. I think it more accurate to say that the proceedings are merely suspended pending the outcome of the contest in the superior court.” However in the same case at page 130, Ritchie, J., holds: “It appears to me that if the Provincial Judge complies with the mandatory direction contained in rule 7 to return all papers touching the matter before him forthwith on receipt of the notice, he is left with nothing upon which to proceed with the case.” The effect of the law as explained by Justice Cooke should not be confused with the provisions of Rule 3.23 which provide a mechanism for the reviewing Court to stay the operation of the decision which is sought to be set aside through the judicial review. The decision in R. v. Hosack (1988), 85 A.R. 98 (Q.B.), deals with the ability of the Court of Justice to take any further steps in the proceeding once notice of an application for judicial review is served upon it. Rule 3.23 deals with the concept of staying the operation of the actual order or decision which is sought to be set aside through the judicial review. 5. Service of the Originating Application for Judicial Review In Tartal v. Alberta (Human Rights Commission), 2023 ABKB 381, 2023 CarswellAlta 1717, Justice Feth said: [2] Rule 3.15(2) of the Alberta Rules of Court, Alta Reg 124/2010 requires that an Originating Application for Judicial Review seeking to set aside a decision must be filed and served within six months of the date of that decision, and Rule 3.15(3) requires that the Originating Application must be served on the decision-maker and “every person or body directly affected by the application.” … [30] The Alberta Court of Appeal recently confirmed that an Originating Application for Judicial Review may be struck when the 6-month time limit for filing and serving the Originating Application is not satisfied: Julien v Alberta (Appeals Commission for Alberta Workers' Compensation), 2023 ABCA 81 at para 16. [31] Alternatively, the failure to comply with the limitation period in Rule 3.15(2) can invite summary dismissal under Rule 7.3(1)(b): Neilson v Leduc (County), 2021 ABQB 735 at paras 22-23; Boll v Woodlands County, 2021 ABQB 406 at para 73; ENMAX Corporation v Alberta (Labour Relations Board), 2018 ABQB 431 at para 30; Athabasca Chipewyan First Nation v Alberta (Minister of Energy), 2009 ABQB 576, affirmed 2011 ABCA 29 [Athabasca CA] at para 25, leave to appeal dismissed [2011] SCCA No 128. …. [33] Compliance with Rule 3.15 is mandatory and the six-month time period to both file and serve the Originating Application cannot be extended or varied: Julien at para 6; Yuill v Alberta (Workers’ Compensation Appeals Commission), 2016 ABQB 369 at paras 75 and 78; ENMAX at para 13 and 30; Boll at para 68. Failure to either file or serve within the limitation period is fatal and the desired remedy - setting aside the decision - cannot be granted. …. [43] While the Interpretation Act applies generally to Alberta enactments, including statutes and regulations, Rule 1.8(b) states that s 22(7) of the Interpretation Act does not apply to the Rules of Court. [44] The calculation of the six-month time limit in Rule 3.15(2) for filing and serving the Originating Application is instead determined by Rule 13.4(1): When counting to or from a date in months, time is calculated from the date on which the event or activity occurs in the month to the same-numbered day in a subsequent or previous month, as the case requires. [45] The Alberta Court of Appeal previously confirmed, under the predecessor to Rule 3.15(2), that “the six-month limitation runs from the date of the decision”: Athabasca CA at para 27. …. [47] Rule 13.15 states that a document is filed when the court clerk of the judicial centre acknowledges on the document that the document is filed in the action. Under Rule 13.14, when the court clerk is “presented” with a commencement document (such as an Originating Application for Judicial Review), the clerk must endorse on the document the action number assigned to the action and stamp the document with the date it is filed. …. [49] The court clerk’s endorsement of an action number and a filing stamp on a commencement document starts the action or proceeding, authenticates the document, and represents to the world that the action or proceeding exists and the technical rules are materially in compliance. [50] Rule 3.15(2) requires the Originating Application to be “filed and served within 6 months.” The obligation is sequential: after filing the Originating Application, the filed commencement document must be served within the same six-month period. Service of the filed document clarifies for the recipient that the proceeding is not just intended, but has been started, and describes the claim definitively. Further, the court clerk’s endorsement confirms that the document is authentic, provides the court number for tracking the action or proceeding, and confirms compliance with the technical rules. [51] Rule 3.15(2) is interpreted consistently with the foundational principles expressed in Rule 1.2, which promote expeditious and cost-effective process. Requiring timely service of the filed document promotes efficiency. The respondent need not wait indefinitely for a filed version and may proceed in responding to the application without delay. …. [54] The service requirement in Rule 3.15(2) is substantive in nature, not procedural: ENMAX at para 28. An applicant is obliged to follow the prescribed procedure. A “courtesy copy of an originating application does not equate to service”: ENMAX at para 19. An unfiled version of an Originating Application does not attest to an existing proceeding and leaves uncertainty about the scope of the claim, which might change before filing. Mere knowledge of an action does not constitute service: Al-Ghamdi v Alberta, 2017 ABQB 169 at para 7. [55] Moreover, Rules 1.5(5) and 3.15(2) expressly prohibit extending the limitation period for the service of judicial review applications. 6. Rule 3.15(3)(b)—“as the circumstances require” In Sedgwick v. Edmonton Real Estate Board Co-Operative Listing Bureau Limited, 2021 ABQB 59, 2021 CarswellAlta 121, affirmed 2022 ABCA 264, Justice Mandziuk said: [38] I interpret the phrase “as the circumstances require” in 3.15(3)(b) as a reference to the provincial or federal levels of government rather than as an importation of discretion with respect to serving the notice: Silver Willow Water Co-op Ltd v Vermillion River (County), 2018 ABQB 952 at para 8. In Silver Willow Water Co-op Ltd. v. Vermillion River (County), 2018 ABQB 952, 2018 CarswellAlta 2761, an application for judicial review was served on neither the Minister of Justice and Solicitor General nor the Attorney General for Canada. The applicant submitted that the phrase “as the circumstances require” found in R. 3.15(3)(b) meant that in some circumstances it was permissible to serve neither of the “Minister of Justice and Solicitor General” nor the “Attorney General for Canada”. Justice Michalyshyn did not agree. His Lordship said: [7] Mr. Armstrong argues that, in the circumstances, the parenthetical “as circumstances require” can be read to exclude the need to serve either the Minister of Justice and Solicitor General or the Attorney General for Canada. [8] I agree however with Mr. Solowan that, in the circumstances here, the phrase “as circumstances require” informs which of those bodies need be served, not if either of them must be served. 7. Rule 3.15(3)(c)—“Directly affected” In Hazkar Developments Inc. v. Cochrane (Town), 2019 ABQB 552, 2019 CarswellAlta 1485, 54 Admin. L.R. (6th) 322, Justice McCarthy discussed the meaning of the words “directly affected” as they are found in the Rule. His Lordship said: [44] I have been provided with no authority that defines “directly affected” in the context of the Alberta Rules. The Court in Enmax provides some useful guidance: that if a party is directly affected by the original decision, they will likely be directly affected by the outcome of a subsequent judicial review application: at para 12. However, the question remains how does a Court determine if and how a person is directly affected by a decision. [45] The words “directly affected” must be interpreted restrictively: Normtek at paras 52–56; Friends of the Athabasca at 4; Re Endowed at 483; McIver at paras 20-21. In these cases, the Court set out that the legislature clearly intended to limit the number of persons who must be notified of judicial review applications. The adverb “directly” excludes everyone who has been indirectly affected and who has a mere general or community interest. However, this does not mean that the Court requires “proof of substantive rights that would be directly affected”, as suggested by Hazkar. 8. Certiorari and Prohibition Distinguished In Morawetz v. Alberta (Director of SafeRoads), 2024 ABKB 588, Justice Marion said: [52] Certiorari is available as a “general remedy of supervision of the machinery of government decision-making. The order may go to any public body with power to decide any matter affecting the rights, interests, property, privileges or liberty of any person”: Martineau v Matsqui Institution, 1979 CanLII 184 (SCC), [1980] 1 SCR 602 at p 628; May v Ferndale Institution, 2005 SCC 82 at para 26; Medical Laboratory Consultants Corp v Calgary Regional Health Authority, 2002 ABQB 200 at para 16. It lies to compel an administrative tribunal to provide the record of proceedings, typically with a request to quash the decision: ALRI Report p 16. [53] Prohibition, on the other hand, allows a superior court to prevent a tribunal from acting or continuing to act on an inquiry that it is not entitled to take: Calgary (City) v Alberta (Human Rights and Citizenship Commission), 2011 ABCA 65 at para 23; Paquette v Canada, 1987 ABCA 188 para 68 (dissenting on other grounds); ALRI Report at 16-17; Sara Blake, Administrative Law in Canada, 7th ed (Toronto: LexisNexis Canada, 2022) at 248. It has been described as preventing proceedings or orders from being made: Guy Régimbald, Canadian Administrative Law, 3rd ed (Markham: LexisNexis Canada, 2021) at 583. 9. Style of Cause for an Order in the Nature of Certiorari In Brewer v. Fraser Milner Casgrain LLP, 2008 ABCA 160, 2008 CarswellAlta 554, 432 A.R. 188, 90 Alta. L.R. (4th) 201, an issue arose as to “whether, and to what extent, a tribunal created by statute can appeal from a superior court's judicial review quashing that tribunal's decision.” The Chief Commissioner of the Alberta Human Rights and Citizenship Commission contended that he could appeal a Queen's Bench order which quashed one of his decisions. On the matter of the style of cause in an application for an order in the nature of certiorari, Côté J.A., said at pp. 208–210: 15 Alberta's present Rules of Court replace the former notice of motion for certiorari with an originating notice for judicial review to quash (R. 753.03, passed in 1987). Before that, the Rules had expressly replaced the old writ of certiorari with that notice of motion for certiorari (1914, R. 824). 16 However, those two Rules amendments merely altered the forms and the precise document to commence proceedings. Neither they, nor any statute, creates or created any cause of action or right to quash. That is still governed by the common law (as modified by fairly recent case law). These 20th century changes in procedure have no effect on the rights of any of the persons involved. See R. v. Titchmarsh (1915), 22 D.L.R. 272, 32 O.L.R. 569 (C.A.); cf. Re McEwen, [1941] 1 W.W.R. 129, 140-41 Man. C.A.; affd., [1941] S.C.R. 542; cf. R. v. Batchelor, [1978] 2 S.C.R. 988, 18 N.R. 416, at para. 42–46. So the substantive law on quashing by judicial review is the common law on quashing by certiorari (with certain modern modifications). 17 What was the common-law writ of certiorari? 18 The word certiorari is just Latin for “to be better informed”. For centuries the writ of certiorari issuing from a superior court, was virtually the only way that justices of the peace and other tribunals (other than superior courts) received any form of review or control. English substantive rights often flowed from writs and their procedure. 19 The key feature of certiorari was a command by the monarch to the Justices of Peace or other tribunal to give up the case to, and send their entire record to, the superior court. Once thus “better informed”, the superior court could either quash the decision of the tribunal, or send the record back and tell the inferior tribunal to proceed. See R. v. Titchmarsh, supra, at 277-78; de Smith, Judicial Review of Admin. Action 373–76, 388-89 (2d ed. 1968). (Recent editions of de Smith are briefer.) Where judicial review is sought to quash the decision below, Alberta Rules still order the tribunal to send up the record: Rr. 753.12 and 753.13. 20 Since the Chief Commissioner here puts weight on the style of cause used in the Court of Queen's Bench, we must examine the common-law practice as to parties. 21 The authoritative text was Chitty's Forms of Proceedings in the King's Bench Division. It is consistent from the 11th edition of 1879 through the 14th edition of 1912. Its wording for the writ of certiorari is as follows: GEORGE THE FIFTH by the Grace of God, … to the judge of the county court of , holden at , greeting: We, willing for certain causes to be certified of a plaint levied in our court before you … command you that you send to us forthwith at the King's Bench Division of our High Court of Justice the said plaint aforesaid, with all things touching the same … that we may further cause to be done thereupon what of right we shall see fit to be done. Witness , Lord High Chancellor of Great Britain … 22 See also Parker L.J., 11 Hals. Laws 124-25 (para. 230) (3d ed. 1955). The writ of certiorari has no style of cause in the modern sense. If one wanted to draw up a Queen's Bench style of cause for the originating notice here, based on the common law, it would read as follows: Her Majesty the Queen, at the relation of Janice Brewer Applicant—and—The Chief Commissioner of the Alberta Human Rights andCitizenship Commission Respondent Doubtless Messrs. Fraser Milner could then move and getthemselves added as a second respondent. It is customary inAlberta to skip Her Majesty as the nominal applicant andmerely name the relator (Brewer) as the applicant. (Rules 739(3) and 753.09 are vague and ambiguous on the parties to judicial review.) 23 The critical point is that the common law writ (or the notice of motion or originating notice which replaces it) names the statutory tribunal in order to get that tribunal's file. The tribunal is not a party in the traditional sense. Indeed after service of the writ (or notice of motion), the tribunal below gives up its file and loses jurisdiction over the case: R. v. Batchelor, supra. In Canada the tribunal rarely if ever pays costs, even if its decision is quashed. 24 Nor does the tribunal even have to be a party. That was expressly held in Syncrude Can. v. I.D. #189 (1986), 70 A.R. 211, 213, ¶¶ 12, 15. It especially need not be named as a respondent if it has already delivered up its record: R. v. Christie McKay & Co., [1992] 4 W.W.R. 151, 152, 80 Man. R. (2d) 76, ¶ 3; affd. [1993] 3 W.W.R. 396, 398-99, 83 Man. R. (2d) 197 (C.A.). (Indeed there is authority that the tribunal should not be named as a respondent to a motion for judicial review of its decision: dictum in Gratton v. Cdn. Judicial Council (1994), 115 D.L.R. (4th) 81, 89d, 78 F.T.R. 214, citing A.-G. Can. v. Bernard (Cdn. Human Rights Trib.), [1994] 2 F.C. 447, 17 Admin L.R. (2d) 2, 164 N.R. 361 (F.C.A.). Whether that authority is distinguishable in Alberta is not clear; the Bernard case cites Federal Court of Canada Rules, some just like Alberta's Rules, some different.) 25 One can sue an individual over a disputed title to land without making the Registrar of Land Titles a party, or appeal from a lower court without making the lower court or its judge a party. At the end, the superior court (or appeal court) can order the Registrar of Land Titles or the lower court to conform to the superior court's judgment, though they are not parties. 26 I do not suggest that this history proves that the Chief Commissioner cannot appeal. Rather, my point is that the Chief Commissioner is neutral. The fact that it is customary in Alberta to name the tribunal subject to judicial review as a respondent in the Queen's Bench style of cause is merely a historical and logistical feature. It is not a statement for or against any substantive rights or standing of that tribunal. 10. Standards of Review In Telecommunications Workers Union v. Telus Communications Inc., 2013 ABQB 298, Justice Nation discussed the standards of review. At paragraphs 15–18: 15 In Dunsmuir v. New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9, 1 SCR 190, the Supreme Court of Canada attempted to clarify what it referred to at para. 1 as “the troubling question of the approach to be taken in judicial review of decisions of administrative tribunals”. The Supreme Court held in that case that there are two standards of review: reasonableness and the less deferential standard of correctness. 16 The Court in Dunsmuir at paras. 54 to 58 set out guidance relating to questions that, under existing law, will be reviewed on a reasonableness standard. A reasonableness standard (or deference) is usually the case where a tribunal is interpreting its own statute or statutes closely connected to its function. Computing the Limitation Date The wording of rule 753.11 which employs the term “after” does not make a difference to the computation of time since s. 22(7) of the Interpretation Act specifies that it applies when anything is to be done within a time “after, from, of or before a specified day”. By the wording of that section, the key date which controls the computation of time is the “specified day”. In this case, the specified day is the day the decision was received by Becker, namely, October 27, 1997. Section 22(8) specifically sets out what is included when counting numbers of months after or before a specified day. It provides at s. 22(8)(a) that the period shall be reckoned as limited by and including the day immediately after the specified day and “the day in the last month” is set out in s. 22(8)(b) as “having the same calendar number as the specified day”. In this case, therefore, the last month is April and the day having the same calendar number as the specified day is the 27th. Becker v. Alberta (Director of Employment Standards) (2000), 277 A.R. 131 (C.A.), at 135-136, per curiam. 22. Time Cannot Be Extended In Julien v. Alberta (Appeals Commission for Alberta Workers’ Compensation), 2023 ABCA 81, 2023 CarswellAlta 590, the Court said, at paragraph 6: [6] As the chambers judge noted, compliance with Rule 3.15 is mandatory, and the six-month time period to file and serve cannot be extended: Baker v Drouin, 2017 ABQB 204 at paras 11-17; ENMAX Corporation v Alberta (Labour Relations Board), 2018 ABQB 431 at para 13; Boll v Woodlands County, 2021 ABQB 406 at para 68; Neilson v Leduc (County), 2021 ABQB 735 at paras 26-27. The Court also noted that section 10 of the Judicature Act does not apply: [15] In particular, and contrary to the suggestion of Mr. Julien, courts have no jurisdiction under s 10 (“Relief against forfeiture”) of the Judicature Act to extend, or otherwise provide relief from, a time limit imposed by a statute or the Rules of Court. Equitable jurisdiction under s 10 does not apply to penalties or forfeitures imposed by statute, or to questions of civil procedure: Tamglass American Inc. v Richter, Allen & Taylor, Inc., 2005 ABCA 341 at paras 20-24; Post v Kellogg Brown & Root (Canada) Company, 2005 ABCA 390 at para 7; Hansraj v Ao, 2004 ABCA 223 at para 64. 23. Rule 3.15 applies to criminal cases and the 6 month deadline cannot be extended In R. v. Lindstrom, 2024 ABKB 678, Justice Anderson held that 3.15 applies to applications in relation to criminal matters and that the deadline set out in R. 3.15(2) cannot be extended. His Lordship said: [12] Rule 3.15 of the Alberta Rules of Court mandates the applicable procedure with respect to applications for certiorari. The Rule provides that an application for certiorari must be filed and served within six months after the date of the challenged decision or act. Rule 3.15(2) provides that the time for filing and service of the application cannot be varied. Thus, Rule 3.15(2) establishes a limitation period which the Court has no discretion to extend: Chaudhary v Alberta, 2023 ABCA 254 at para 7; Julien v Alberta, 2023 ABCA 81. [13] The Court of Queen's Bench of Alberta Criminal Procedure Rules, SI/2017-76, (2017) C Gaz II, vol 151 no 25 [the Alberta Criminal Rules] came into force on December 13, 2017. [14] Rule 3.15 of the Alberta Rules of Court applies to criminal cases because Rule 11(1)(a) of the Alberta Criminal Rules specifically directs that Part 3, Division 2, Subdivision 2 of the Alberta Rules of Court are to apply to applications for certiorari in criminal cases. Rule 3.15(2) is contained within this subdivision and is therefore incorporated by reference into Alberta Criminal Rule 11(1). …. [16] For these reasons, the six-month deadline for filing and serving a certiorari application contained in Rule 3.15(2) applies to criminal cases. The Court has no discretion to extend this deadline. …. [41] I conclude that the deadline found in Rule 3.15(2) which has been incorporated by reference into the Alberta Criminal Rules is applicable to certiorari applications relating to criminal matters. For this reason, there is no jurisdiction to extend the time to file a certiorari application in a criminal case beyond the six months specified in Rule 3.15(2).
paragraphs.heading: Alberta Rules of Court – Rule 3 (Part 2)

sentences.text: Commentary § 3.15:1 Rule 3.15 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta.
Reg.
Rule applies to municipal bylaws In Okotoks (Town) v.
Foothills (Municipal District) No.
31, 2013 ABCA 222, the Court said, at paragraph 9: 9 … First, Okotoks submits that the enactment of a bylaw is not a “decision or act” of a body; hence Rule 3.15(2) does not apply.
In our view, the Rule should not be read so narrowly.
A municipal council can only act by resolution or bylaw: MGA section 180.
Accordingly, we conclude that a bylaw is a decision or act of the municipality subject to the remedies in Rules 3.15(1)(a) and (b).
In so holding, mindful of the nature of those remedies, we are not to be taken to have suggested that there exists some wide-ranging power to review the substance of bylaws for “reasonableness”.
Domestic tribunals In Falk v.
Calgary Real Estate Board Co-Operative Ltd., 2000 ABQB 296, 2000 CarswellAlta 428, 265 A.R.
60, 82 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 201, the plaintiff was “subject to the Board's tribunals by virtue of the voluntary contractual relationship between herself and the Board.
Therefore, the Board's disciplinary tribunals are of a private or domestic nature” (p.
On the question of whether the judicial review provisions in the Rules of Court apply to consensual (domestic) tribunals, Rowbotham, J. said, at p.
66: I find that although the Board's disciplinary tribunals are domestic, their decisions are subject to judicial review for the limited purposes discussed in [Kaplan v.
Canadian Institute of Actuaries (1994), 161 A.R.
268 (C.A.); additional reasons at (1998), 212 A.R.
L.R.
(3d) 251 (C.A.); leave to appeal refused (1998), 227 N.R.

The court is entitled to review the decisions to determine whether the tribunals have acted within their jurisdiciton; to ensure that decisions within their jurisdiction are not patently unreasonable; and to prevent breaches of natural justice or fairness.
In Homestead Housing Co-operative Ltd. v.
Barth, 2016 ABQB 538, 2016 CarswellAlta 1916 (Master), Master Schlosser said: 26 Can a private organization be judicially reviewed?

Manderscheid J, in Slovenian Canadian (at para 29), after a review of authority, tells us that the Court can conduct a limited judicial review to determine whether (in that case) the Association violated its by-laws.

In Lee v Yeung, Macklin J said (paras 29–31): 29 Despite the historical distinction between public and private law remedies, the courts have interpreted the Rules of Court as giving teeth to the declaratory remedy in the private law context.
In Kaplan v Canadian Institute of Actuaries, 161 AR 321, [1994] A.J.

No 868 (QB), Hunt J stated: 44 It seems to me that even if certiorari will not lie against a consensual tribunal, the court possesses broad enough powers under Rule 753.05 to grant the remedy it considers appropriate to the particular case, including the setting aside of an invalid decision or action … 30 In Falk v Calgary Real Estate Board Co-operative Ltd, 2000 ABQB 296, 265 AR 60, Rowbotham J considered Hunt J's reasoning in Kaplan and concluded: 13 I find that although the Board's disciplinary tribunals are domestic, their decisions are subject to judicial review for the limited purposes discussed in Kaplan, supra.

The court is entitled to review the decisions to determine whether the tribunals have acted within their jurisdiction; to ensure that decisions within their jurisdiction are not patently unreasonable; and to prevent breaches of natural justice or fairness.
In this case the decisions in question were within both tribunals' jurisdictions.

Therefore, the substantive issue is whether these decisions should be set aside as being patently unreasonable; and to prevent breaches of natural justice or fairness …[Emphasis added] 31 Accordingly it appears that while, historically, judicial review was only available as a public law remedy, Knox does confirm that private bodies are prima facie only subject to private law remedies.
Kaplan and Falk emphasize that judicial review is available in relation to decisions of private bodies for limited purposes.
And now see: Wall v Judicial Committee of the Highwood Congregation of Jehovah's Witnesses (Wakeling JA, dissenting).
27 These cases leave no doubt that a limited judicial review of the decision of this private organization is available.
Service of application In Sedgwick v.

Edmonton Real Estate Board Co-Operative Listing Bureau Limited, 2021 ABQB 59, 2021 CarswellAlta 121, affirmed 2022 ABCA 264, Justice Mandziuk found that service had not been effected as required by Rule 3.15(3)(b), and said: [39] There is no evidence before me that this notice was given.
That would seem to represent a full stop to the application for judicial review (at least at this point).

This is consistent with Graesser, J's decision in Peter Lehmann Wines Ltd v Vintage West Wine Marketing Inc, 2015 ABQB 481: lack of service on the Crown precluded a mandamus remedy “[b]ecause a Crown or statutory body is always implicated in administrative law, Rule 3.15(3)(b) … requires the Minister of Justice and Solicitor General for Alberta to be given notice of applications which ask the Court to contemplate any of the prerogative writs used to initiate a judicial review” (at para 47).
[40] The relief sought here is prerogative in nature insofar as it arises from the judicial review argument.
Therefore, the notice must be given.
In ENMAX Corporation v.
Alberta (Labour Relations Board), 2018 ABQB 431, 2018 CarswellAlta 1089, ENMAX filed an application (“the application”) for judicial review of a decision of the Alberta Labour Relations Board.

ENMAX did not serve notice of the application upon the Association of Professional Engineers and Geoscientists of Alberta (APEGA) which had successfully obtained intervenor status in the application before the Board.
Unions which had been served with notice of the application sought to have the application dismissed on the basis that APEGA had not been served.
APEGA (which had received a “courtesy copy” of the application) had decided not to participate in the application; the Unions were relying on a deficiency about which APEGA did not care.
Justice Hunt McDonald concluded that the obligation to serve notice of the application on APEGA as a “body directly affected by the application” was mandatory and could not be waived.

Her Ladyship summarily dismissed ENMAX's application for judicial review, and said: 15 ENMAX claims that the Unions are trying to take unfair advantage of an alleged service irregularity, and highlights the fact that APEGA and the EITs are not the complaining parties.

ENMAX states, “That a party did not receive a copy of the claim or received it by means other than those described in Part 11 of the Alberta Rules of Court is not determinative.” ENMAX argues that APEGA and the EITs had knowledge of the general nature of the ENMAX Application within the six-month limitation period, and this knowledge is sufficient to satisfy the policy reasons and purpose of the Rules.

16 ENMAX claims that to interpret rule 3.15 to require formal service on APEGA and the EITs leads to an absurd result because it frustrates the purpose of the Rules and leads to an unfair or unreasonable result.
ENMAX states that formal service would not have altered the interest or participation level of APEGA or the EITs.
17 The object of service is a relevant consideration: Condominium Plan 9812082 v Battistella Developments Inc, 2014 ABQB 644 at para 11.
However, I disagree with the assertion by ENMAX that establishing notice of an application for judicial review is sufficient.
18 An applicant has an obligation to follow legislated procedure: Raczynska v Alberta (Human Rights Commission), 2015 ABQB 494 at para 63.
Rule 3.15(3) states that an originating application for judicial review must be served on every person or body directly affected by the application.
This is a mandatory requirement.
Rule 3.15 does not allow for discretion and does not differentiate between affected parties that oppose or support an application.
19 Knowledge of an application is not equivalent to service, even if there is knowledge of the general nature of the application.

Furthermore, this court has previously found that a courtesy copy of an originating application does not equate to service: Lynne M Miller v Chief of the Commission and Tribunals, Alberta Human Rights Commission and The Workers' Compensation Board (27 January 2015), Calgary, 1401 045218 (ABQB).
20 In Raczynska, Justice Graesser acknowledged that the strict application of rule 3.15 may be viewed as harsh: at para 76.

In Zimmer-Worker Estate v Alberta (Appeals Commission for Alberta Workers' Compensation) (7 October 2015), Edmonton, 1403-00907 (ABQB), Justice Simpson agreed at paragraph 28: […] this Court has no jurisdiction to provide relief by way of extending the Applicant time for naming and serving under the Workers Compensation Act or the Alberta Rules of Court.
I agree with Graesser J's comment in Raczynska that this is a harsh position.

However, until the legislature amends the legislation or our Court of Appeal provides authority to this Court by reference to the Judicature Act or otherwise it is not open for this Court to apply the Judicature Act and provide any relief regarding the requirements in the statue or the rules.
21 The fact that APEGA and the EITs had knowledge of the general nature of the ENMAX Application does not satisfy the mandatory service requirement in rule 3.15(3).
Whether or not formal service would have altered the interest or participation level of APEGA or the EITs is irrelevant.
This strict interpretation of the Rules may seem harsh but that does not mean the result is absurd or unreasonable.
Can a party directly affected by an application waive the service obligation in rule 3.15?
22 Counsel for APEGA informed counsel for ENMAX that APEGA is interested in the outcome of the judicial review but is not interested in participating.
Mr.
Chai, spokesperson for the EITs, confirmed that the EITs are not interested in participating in the ENMAX Application since the position of the EITs aligns with and is represented by ENMAX.
23 ENMAX argues that benefitting parties may waive the benefits of a statute and that the intention to waive a right may be expressed in an informal fashion or inferred from conduct.
ENMAX claims that by their advice and actions, APEGA and the EITs unilaterally and unequivocally waived the service requirement and the limitation period of rule 3.15.
The Unions argue that APEGA and the EITs may waive their right to participate in the ENMAX Application but they cannot waive the applicant's mandatory service obligations.
24 In MacDonald v Royal Trust Corporation of Canada

(1984), 54 AR 116 (ABQB) [MacDonald], Justice Brennan stated the general rule of waiver at para 12: It has long been established, that generally speaking, a person may waive the benefits of a statute unless to do so would be contrary to public policy; and such waiver is not contrary to public policy where the rights, privileges or advantages conferred by the statute are for the benefit of the individual in his private capacity as opposed to being for the benefit of the public as a whole.
[citations omitted] 25 The applicants in the case were seeking a declaration pursuant to section 10(1) of the Interest Act, RSC c I-18, regarding the prepayment of a mortgage.
The applicants had signed a contract renewing the mortgage; the contract was found to waive the beneficial prepayment provisions of the Interest Act.
26 In Heikkila v Alberta (Workers' Compensation Board, Appeals Commission), 2003 ABQB 544, Justice Hawco considered whether the respondents had waived the limitation defence.
He decided the facts of the case did not establish that either of the respondents waived the limitation period of former rule 753.
He did not discuss whether the respondents could have waived the applicant's service obligation.

27 In U(J) v Alberta (Director of Child Welfare), 2001 ABCA 125, the applicant failed to file a copy of the notice of appeal in the Provincial Court as was required under the Child Welfare Act, SA 1984, c C-8.1.
The applicant asked the chambers judge to exercise parens patria jurisdiction to allow the appeal to proceed despite her non-compliance with the filing requirement.
The Court of Appeal stated that the court does not have the jurisdiction to waive a statutory limitation period or a statutory filing requirement: at para 6.

The Court of Appeal also said that the absence of a provision to allow the waiver of a statutory requirement does not mean there is a gap in the legislation: “if it was intended that such requirements could be overridden, the mandatory aspect of the legislation would be superfluous”: at para 7.
28 In MacDonald the general rule regarding waiver was found to apply to a prepayment rule that a mortgagor may be able to benefit from.
In contrast, rule 3.15 imposes a mandatory obligation on the applicant.
As with the filing requirement in U(J) and the limitation period in Heikkila, the service requirement in rule 3.15 is substantive in nature.

29 Rule 3.15 does not address waiver and I am not aware of a case that specifically considers whether a party directly affected by an application for judicial review may waive the applicant's service obligation.
Considering the above cases and the strict interpretation of rule 3.15 previously noted, I agree with the Unions
APEGA and the EITs may waive their right to participate in the proceedings but they cannot waive ENMAX's mandatory service obligations.
In Kyambadde v.
Calgary Police Service, 2024 ABKB 370, the Minister of Justice was not served with the originating application for judicial review.
It was another person directly affected by the judicial review application who raised the issue.
Justice Poelman said: [13] One might be sympathetic with the Minister not being served.
Even now, the Minister declines to be involved.
How the Minister responds, however, is not determinative.

A Crown or statutory body always is implicated in administrative law and thus must be given notice of applications that ask the court to contemplate a judicial review; an order cannot be granted without such notice: Peter Lehmann Wines Ltd v Vintage West Wine Marketing Inc, 2015 ABQB 481 at paras 47 and 48
ENMAX Corporation v Alberta (Labour Relations Board), 2018 ABQB 431 at para 29.
Service of notice of the application suspends proceedings in the Alberta Court of Justice In R. v.
Hosack (1988), 85 A.R.

98 (Q.B.), Justice Cooke said that if an application is made in the Court of King's Bench for judicial review of a decision made by a judge of the Provincial Court of Alberta (now a Justice of the Alberta Court of Justice), then upon service of notice of the application on the Court of Justice, that Court's jurisdiction to act in the matter is suspended.
His Lordship said: [18] The Supreme Court of Canada in the case of R. v.
Batchelor (1977), 1978 CanLII 35 (SCC), 18 N.R.
2d) 113, makes it clear that the lower Court's jurisdiction to act is dormant from the time of service of the writ as opposed to the time of the return to the writ.

Laskin, C.J.C., at 128 C.C.C. states: “It seems to me that, however the matter is regarded, there must be a suspension of jurisdiction when an application to quash or a combined application to prohibit and to quash is served on the inferior Court with the command, under the Rules, to make a return forthwith.

The Judge, compelled to make the return, cannot, unless he risks disobedience with its attendant consequences, go on with the matter before him until the application to the superior Court is disposed of by dismissal thereof. … [30] At page 128 of the Batchelor case, Laskin, C.J.C., states: “As put by Letourneau, The Prerogative Writs in Canadian Criminal Law and Procedure

161: ‘… in criminal law, the transmission the record of the proceedings of the superior court, as required to be made forthwith by most rules of court on an application for certiorari, in fact operates as a stay of proceedings. “The author goes on to say that the inferior court is deprived of its jurisdiction to resume the proceedings as, after the removal, nothing is left before it.

I think it more accurate to say that the proceedings are merely suspended pending the outcome of the contest in the superior court.” However in the same case at page 130, Ritchie, J., holds: “It appears to me that if the Provincial Judge complies with the mandatory direction contained in rule 7 to return all papers touching the matter before him forthwith on receipt of the notice, he is left with nothing upon which to proceed with the case.” The effect of the law as explained by Justice Cooke should not be confused with the provisions of Rule 3.23 which provide a mechanism for the reviewing Court to stay the operation of the decision which is sought to be set aside through the judicial review.
The decision in R. v.
Hosack (1988), 85 A.R.
98 (Q.B.), deals with the ability of the Court of Justice to take any further steps in the proceeding once notice of an application for judicial review is served upon it.
Rule 3.23 deals with the concept of staying the operation of the actual order or decision which is sought to be set aside through the judicial review.
Service of the Originating Application for Judicial Review In Tartal v.

Alberta (Human Rights Commission), 2023 ABKB 381, 2023 CarswellAlta 1717, Justice Feth said: [2] Rule 3.15(2) of the Alberta Rules of Court, Alta Reg 124/2010 requires that an Originating Application for Judicial Review seeking to set aside a decision must be filed and served within six months of the date of that decision, and Rule 3.15(3) requires that the Originating Application must be served on the decision-maker and “every person or body directly affected by the application.” … [30] The Alberta Court of Appeal recently confirmed that an Originating Application for Judicial Review may be struck when the 6-month time limit for filing and serving the Originating Application is not satisfied: Julien v Alberta (Appeals Commission for Alberta Workers' Compensation), 2023 ABCA 81 at para 16.
[31] Alternatively, the failure to comply with the limitation period in Rule 3.15(2) can invite summary dismissal under Rule 7.3(1)(b): Neilson v Leduc (County), 2021 ABQB 735 at paras 22-23
Boll v Woodlands County, 2021 ABQB 406 at para 73
ENMAX Corporation v Alberta (Labour Relations Board), 2018 ABQB 431 at para 30
Athabasca Chipewyan First Nation v Alberta (Minister of Energy), 2009 ABQB 576, affirmed 2011 ABCA 29 [Athabasca CA] at para 25, leave to appeal dismissed [2011] SCCA No 128. ….
[33] Compliance with Rule 3.15 is mandatory and the six-month time period to both file and serve the Originating Application cannot be extended or varied: Julien at para 6
Yuill v Alberta (Workers’ Compensation Appeals Commission), 2016 ABQB 369 at paras 75 and 78
ENMAX at para 13 and 30
Boll at para 68.
Failure to either file or serve within the limitation period is fatal and the desired remedy - setting aside the decision - cannot be granted. ….

[43] While the Interpretation Act applies generally to Alberta enactments, including statutes and regulations, Rule 1.8(b) states that s 22(7) of the Interpretation Act does not apply to the Rules of Court.

[44] The calculation of the six-month time limit in Rule 3.15(2) for filing and serving the Originating Application is instead determined by Rule 13.4(1): When counting to or from a date in months, time is calculated from the date on which the event or activity occurs in the month to the same-numbered day in a subsequent or previous month, as the case requires.
[45] The Alberta Court of Appeal previously confirmed, under the predecessor to Rule 3.15(2), that “the six-month limitation runs from the date of the decision”: Athabasca CA at para 27. ….
[47] Rule 13.15 states that a document is filed when the court clerk of the judicial centre acknowledges on the document that the document is filed in the action.

Under Rule 13.14, when the court clerk is “presented” with a commencement document (such as an Originating Application for Judicial Review), the clerk must endorse on the document the action number assigned to the action and stamp the document with the date it is filed. ….

[49] The court clerk’s endorsement of an action number and a filing stamp on a commencement document starts the action or proceeding, authenticates the document, and represents to the world that the action or proceeding exists and the technical rules are materially in compliance.

[50] Rule 3.15(2) requires the Originating Application to be “filed and served within 6 months.” The obligation is sequential: after filing the Originating Application, the filed commencement document must be served within the same six-month period.
Service of the filed document clarifies for the recipient that the proceeding is not just intended, but has been started, and describes the claim definitively.
Further, the court clerk’s endorsement confirms that the document is authentic, provides the court number for tracking the action or proceeding, and confirms compliance with the technical rules.
[51] Rule 3.15(2) is interpreted consistently with the foundational principles expressed in Rule 1.2, which promote expeditious and cost-effective process.
Requiring timely service of the filed document promotes efficiency.
The respondent need not wait indefinitely for a filed version and may proceed in responding to the application without delay. ….
[54] The service requirement in Rule 3.15(2) is substantive in nature, not procedural: ENMAX at para 28.
An applicant is obliged to follow the prescribed procedure.
A “courtesy copy of an originating application does not equate to service”: ENMAX at para 19.
An unfiled version of an Originating Application does not attest to an existing proceeding and leaves uncertainty about the scope of the claim, which might change before filing.
Mere knowledge of an action does not constitute service: Al-Ghamdi v Alberta, 2017 ABQB 169 at para 7.
[55] Moreover, Rules 1.5(5) and 3.15(2) expressly prohibit extending the limitation period for the service of judicial review applications.
Rule 3.15(3)(b)—“as the circumstances require” In Sedgwick v.

Edmonton Real Estate Board Co-Operative Listing Bureau Limited, 2021 ABQB 59, 2021 CarswellAlta 121, affirmed 2022 ABCA 264, Justice Mandziuk said: [38] I interpret the phrase “as the circumstances require” in 3.15(3)(b) as a reference to the provincial or federal levels of government rather than as an importation of discretion with respect to serving the notice: Silver Willow Water Co-op Ltd v Vermillion River (County), 2018 ABQB 952 at para 8.
In Silver Willow Water Co-op Ltd. v.

Vermillion River (County), 2018 ABQB 952, 2018 CarswellAlta 2761, an application for judicial review was served on neither the Minister of Justice and Solicitor General nor the Attorney General for Canada.
The applicant submitted that the phrase “as the circumstances require” found in R.
3.15(3)(b) meant that in some circumstances it was permissible to serve neither of the “Minister of Justice and Solicitor General” nor the “Attorney General for Canada”.
Justice Michalyshyn did not agree.
His Lordship said: [7] Mr.

Armstrong argues that, in the circumstances, the parenthetical “as circumstances require” can be read to exclude the need to serve either the Minister of Justice and Solicitor General or the Attorney General for Canada.
[8] I agree however with Mr.
Solowan that, in the circumstances here, the phrase “as circumstances require” informs which of those bodies need be served, not if either of them must be served.
Rule 3.15(3)(c)—“Directly affected” In Hazkar Developments Inc. v.
Cochrane (Town), 2019 ABQB 552, 2019 CarswellAlta 1485, 54 Admin.
L.R.
(6th) 322, Justice McCarthy discussed the meaning of the words “directly affected” as they are found in the Rule.
His Lordship said: [44] I have been provided with no authority that defines “directly affected” in the context of the Alberta Rules.

The Court in Enmax provides some useful guidance: that if a party is directly affected by the original decision, they will likely be directly affected by the outcome of a subsequent judicial review application: at para 12.
However, the question remains how does a Court determine if and how a person is directly affected by a decision.
[45] The words “directly affected” must be interpreted restrictively: Normtek at paras 52–56; Friends of the Athabasca at 4; Re Endowed at 483; McIver at paras 20-21.
In these cases, the Court set out that the legislature clearly intended to limit the number of persons who must be notified of judicial review applications.
The adverb “directly” excludes everyone who has been indirectly affected and who has a mere general or community interest.
However, this does not mean that the Court requires “proof of substantive rights that would be directly affected”, as suggested by Hazkar.
Certiorari and Prohibition Distinguished In Morawetz v.
Alberta (Director of SafeRoads), 2024 ABKB 588, Justice Marion said: [52] Certiorari is available as a “general remedy of supervision of the machinery of government decision-making.

The order may go to any public body with power to decide any matter affecting the rights, interests, property, privileges or liberty of any person”: Martineau v Matsqui Institution, 1979 CanLII 184 (SCC), [1980] 1 SCR 602 at p 628
May v Ferndale Institution, 2005 SCC 82 at para 26
Medical Laboratory Consultants Corp v Calgary Regional Health Authority, 2002 ABQB 200 at para 16.
It lies to compel an administrative tribunal to provide the record of proceedings, typically with a request to quash the decision: ALRI Report p 16.

[53] Prohibition, on the other hand, allows a superior court to prevent a tribunal from acting or continuing to act on an inquiry that it is not entitled to take: Calgary (City) v Alberta (Human Rights and Citizenship Commission), 2011 ABCA 65 at para 23
Paquette v Canada, 1987 ABCA 188 para 68 (dissenting on other grounds)
ALRI Report at 16-17
Sara Blake, Administrative Law in Canada, 7th ed (Toronto: LexisNexis Canada, 2022) at 248.
It has been described as preventing proceedings or orders from being made: Guy Régimbald, Canadian Administrative Law, 3rd ed (Markham: LexisNexis Canada, 2021) at 583.
Style of Cause for an Order in the Nature of Certiorari In Brewer v.
Fraser Milner Casgrain LLP, 2008 ABCA 160, 2008 CarswellAlta 554, 432 A.R.
L.R.

(4th) 201, an issue arose as to “whether, and to what extent, a tribunal created by statute can appeal from a superior court's judicial review quashing that tribunal's decision.” The Chief Commissioner of the Alberta Human Rights and Citizenship Commission contended that he could appeal a Queen's Bench order which quashed one of his decisions.
On the matter of the style of cause in an application for an order in the nature of certiorari, Côté J.A., said at pp.
208–210: 15 Alberta's present Rules of Court replace the former notice of motion for certiorari with an originating notice for judicial review to quash (R.
Before that, the Rules had expressly replaced the old writ of certiorari with that notice of motion for certiorari (1914, R.
16 However, those two Rules amendments merely altered the forms and the precise document to commence proceedings.
Neither they, nor any statute, creates or created any cause of action or right to quash.
That is still governed by the common law (as modified by fairly recent case law).
These 20th century changes in procedure have no effect on the rights of any of the persons involved.
See R. v.
Titchmarsh (1915), 22 D.L.R.
Re McEwen, [1941] 1 W.W.R.
R. v.
Batchelor, [1978] 2 S.C.R.
416, at para.
So the substantive law on quashing by judicial review is the common law on quashing by certiorari (with certain modern modifications).
17 What was the common-law writ of certiorari?
18 The word certiorari is just Latin for “to be better informed”.

For centuries the writ of certiorari issuing from a superior court, was virtually the only way that justices of the peace and other tribunals (other than superior courts) received any form of review or control.
English substantive rights often flowed from writs and their procedure.
19 The key feature of certiorari was a command by the monarch to the Justices of Peace or other tribunal to give up the case to, and send their entire record to, the superior court.
Once thus “better informed”, the superior court could either quash the decision of the tribunal, or send the record back and tell the inferior tribunal to proceed.
See R. v.
Titchmarsh, supra, at 277-78; de Smith, Judicial Review of Admin.
(Recent editions of de Smith are briefer.) Where judicial review is sought to quash the decision below, Alberta Rules still order the tribunal to send up the record: Rr.
20 Since the Chief Commissioner here puts weight on the style of cause used in the Court of Queen's Bench, we must examine the common-law practice as to parties.
21 The authoritative text was Chitty's Forms of Proceedings in the King's Bench Division.
It is consistent from the 11th edition of 1879 through the 14th edition of 1912.

Its wording for the writ of certiorari is as follows: GEORGE THE FIFTH by the Grace of God, … to the judge of the county court of , holden at , greeting: We, willing for certain causes to be certified of a plaint levied in our court before you … command you that you send to us forthwith at the King's Bench Division of our High Court of Justice the said plaint aforesaid, with all things touching the same … that we may further cause to be done thereupon what of right we shall see fit to be done.

While, at first blush, that result may seem harsh, it must be remembered that judicial review is itself an equitable and discretionary remedy; in other words, judicial review—complete with its 6 month time limitation—already provides equitable relief from any harshness resulting from the strict application of law.
The law would hold that the Chief's review of the Director's decision is binding and final.
Judicial review provides a mechanism for having that decision reviewed.
Adding a mechanism to the existing mechanism isn't called for.

23 This court does not discount the possibility that, if a real incapacity for the entire period were proved by an applicant, relief from injustice might be found by applying the disability approach found elsewhere in the law, e.g. that the time limit under the Rule might be suspended as in s.
5 of the Limitations Act.
Time Limits and “Procedural Fairness” It is clear, then, that with respect to the “jurisdictional” argument of applicant, those grounds were raised in time and Rule 753.11 was complied with.

The contest, then, is with respect to applicants' procedural fairness arguments: that they were denied counsel, the right to cross-examine, the right to be present while the Engineers gave evidence and presented argument, and so forth. . . . . .

If preliminary applications on procedural fairness grounds are not appropriately brought before the decision of the tribunal is rendered—for example, because an applicant should not be required to waste the court's time or his own money challenging a procedural deficiency before he finds out whether, in the result, there is [a] practical … need to do so—then it may very well be that the time set out in Rule 753.11 does not begin to run until the tribunal makes its decision, nothwithstanding that the “act” complained of occurred outside of the six-month time limit set out in the rule.

In essence, the hearing and the later decision of the tribunal may amount to a “single transaction”, and any grounds for judicial review arising from the hearing itself may be properly brought, in compliance with rule 753.11, within six months of the rendering of decision by the tribunal.
Friends of the Oldman River Society v.
Assn. of Professional Engineers, Geologists and Geophysicists (Alberta) (1997), 55 Alta.
L.R.
403 per Cooke J.
As to when the limitation period begins to run under then Rule 753.11(1), the Court of Appeal said in Becker v.
Alberta (Director of Employment Standards), 2000 ABCA 329, 2000 CarswellAlta 1539, 277 A.R.
(5th) 41, at p.
133 [A.R.]: This court on November 28, 2000 (unreported) upheld and adopted the reasons of Perras, J. in Edmonton (City) v.
L.A.
Ventures Inc., [1999] A.J.
No.
996 (Q.B.), where he stated that the limitation period in rule 753.11 begins to run as of the date of service of the decision.
Computing the Limitation Date The wording of rule 753.11 which employs the term “after” does not make a difference to the computation of time since s.
22(7) of the Interpretation Act specifies that it applies when anything is to be done within a time “after, from, of or before a specified day”.
By the wording of that section, the key date which controls the computation of time is the “specified day”.
In this case, the specified day is the day the decision was received by Becker, namely, October 27, 1997.
Section 22(8) specifically sets out what is included when counting numbers of months after or before a specified day.
It provides at s.
22(8)(a) that the period shall be reckoned as limited by and including the day immediately after the specified day and “the day in the last month” is set out in s.
22(8)(b) as “having the same calendar number as the specified day”.
In this case, therefore, the last month is April and the day having the same calendar number as the specified day is the 27th.
Becker v.
Alberta (Director of Employment Standards) (2000), 277 A.R.
131 (C.A.), at 135-136, per curiam.
Time Cannot Be Extended In Julien v.

Alberta (Appeals Commission for Alberta Workers’ Compensation), 2023 ABCA 81, 2023 CarswellAlta 590, the Court said, at paragraph 6: [6] As the chambers judge noted, compliance with Rule 3.15 is mandatory, and the six-month time period to file and serve cannot be extended: Baker v Drouin, 2017 ABQB 204 at paras 11-17
ENMAX Corporation v Alberta (Labour Relations Board), 2018 ABQB 431 at para 13
Boll v Woodlands County, 2021 ABQB 406 at para 68
Neilson v Leduc (County), 2021 ABQB 735 at paras 26-27.
The Court also noted that section 10 of the Judicature Act does not apply: [15] In particular, and contrary to the suggestion of Mr.

Julien, courts have no jurisdiction under s 10 (“Relief against forfeiture”) of the Judicature Act to extend, or otherwise provide relief from, a time limit imposed by a statute or the Rules of Court.

Equitable jurisdiction under s 10 does not apply to penalties or forfeitures imposed by statute, or to questions of civil procedure: Tamglass American Inc. v Richter, Allen & Taylor, Inc., 2005 ABCA 341 at paras 20-24
Post v Kellogg Brown & Root (Canada) Company, 2005 ABCA 390 at para 7
Hansraj v Ao, 2004 ABCA 223 at para 64.
Rule 3.15 applies to criminal cases and the 6 month deadline cannot be extended In R. v.
Lindstrom, 2024 ABKB 678, Justice Anderson held that 3.15 applies to applications in relation to criminal matters and that the deadline set out in R.
3.15(2) cannot be extended.
His Lordship said: [12] Rule 3.15 of the Alberta Rules of Court mandates the applicable procedure with respect to applications for certiorari.
The Rule provides that an application for certiorari must be filed and served within six months after the date of the challenged decision or act.
Rule 3.15(2) provides that the time for filing and service of the application cannot be varied.
Thus, Rule 3.15(2) establishes a limitation period which the Court has no discretion to extend: Chaudhary v Alberta, 2023 ABCA 254 at para 7; Julien v Alberta, 2023 ABCA 81.
[13] The Court of Queen's Bench of Alberta Criminal Procedure Rules, SI/2017-76, (2017) C Gaz II, vol 151 no 25 [the Alberta Criminal Rules] came into force on December 13, 2017.

[14] Rule 3.15 of the Alberta Rules of Court applies to criminal cases because Rule 11(1)(a) of the Alberta Criminal Rules specifically directs that Part 3, Division 2, Subdivision 2 of the Alberta Rules of Court are to apply to applications for certiorari in criminal cases.
Rule 3.15(2) is contained within this subdivision and is therefore incorporated by reference into Alberta Criminal Rule 11(1). ….
[16] For these reasons, the six-month deadline for filing and serving a certiorari application contained in Rule 3.15(2) applies to criminal cases.
The Court has no discretion to extend this deadline. ….
[41] I conclude that the deadline found in Rule 3.15(2) which has been incorporated by reference into the Alberta Criminal Rules is applicable to certiorari applications relating to criminal matters.
For this reason, there is no jurisdiction to extend the time to file a certiorari application in a criminal case beyond the six months specified in Rule 3.15(2).

paragraphs.heading: Part 3. Court Actions

sentences.text: Notice to obtain record of proceedings

paragraphs.text: (1) An originating applicant for judicial review who seeks an order to set aside a decision or act must include with the originating application a notice in Form 8, addressed to the person or body who made or possesses the record of proceedings on which the decision or act sought to be set aside is based, to send the record of proceedings to the court clerk named in the notice. (2) The notice must require the following to be sent or an explanation to be provided of why an item cannot be sent: (a) the written record, if any, of the decision or act that is the subject of the originating application for judicial review, (b) the reasons given for the decision or act, if any, (c) the document which started the proceeding, (d) the evidence and exhibits filed with the person or body, if any, and (e) anything else relevant to the decision or act in the possession of the person or body. (3) The Court may add to, dispense with or vary anything required to be sent to the court clerk under this rule.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 3.18:1 Rule 3.18 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.18. What Constitutes the Record? In Alberta, the constitution of the record is set out in rules 753.12 and 753.13(1) of the Rules of Court… What is included in the record is not definitive due to the phrases “all things touching the matter” in rules 753.12(1), 753.13(1) and “all other papers or documents touching the matter” in rule 753.13(1)(d). In these two rules the words, “all things” or “all papers or documents” are qualified by the words “touching the matter”. Broda v. Edmonton (City) (1989), 102 A.R. 255 (Q.B.), at 258, per Trussler J. And Smith J. said: As was held by Miller J. in A.U.P.E. v. Alberta, [1978] 3 W.W.R. 63 (T.D.), the effect of R. 753.12 and 753.13 is to expand the constituent elements of the record: It seems abundantly clear that Rules 743 and 744 [now R. 753.12 and 753.13] were specifically worded to eliminate the restrictions laid down in the Nat Bell case by broadening the material required to be placed before the reviewing court and placed an obligation on the latter tribunal to examine the evidence wherever relevant to the application. However, Miller J. further qualified the scope of these two rules at p. 7 by stating: It seems to me that the logical way of interpreting the wording of Rules 743 and 744 is that the inferior tribunal should only be compelled to produce what they already have on hand at the time of the certiorari application or that which they are specifically required to produce by statute, regulation or agreement. Alberta (Labour Relations Board) v. I.B.E.W., Local 1007 (1991), 83 Alta. L.R. (2d) 253 at 260 (Q.B.).

sentences.text: Sending in certified record of proceedings

paragraphs.text: (1) On receipt of an originating application for judicial review and a notice in accordance with rule 3.18, the person or body named in the notice must, as soon as practicable, (a) comply with the notice and send to the court clerk a certified record of proceedings in Form 9, or (b) provide in Form 9 a written explanation why the notice cannot be complied with or fully complied with. (2) The certified record of proceedings sent to the court clerk under this rule constitutes part of the court file of the originating application. (3) If the Court is not satisfied with the explanation for not sending all or part of the record of proceedings, the Court may order any or all of the following: (a) the person or body to provide a better explanation; (b) the person or body to send a certified copy of a record to the court clerk; (c) the person or body to take any other action the Court considers appropriate.
