paragraphs.text: Commentary § 3.19:1 Rule 3.19 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.19. 1. The Return In IMS Health Canada Ltd. v. Information and Privacy Commissioner, 2005 ABCA 325, 2005 CarswellAlta 1416, 376 A.R. 336, 53 Alta. L.R. (4th) 201, Ritter J.A. discussed what must be returned under Rule 753.13. In that case, the Alberta Information and Privacy Commissioner had decided to investigate certain disclosures made by pharmacies to IMS Health Canada Ltd. (a company that collected and analyzed information concerning health care). IMS sought judicial review of the Commissioner's decision, and a dispute arose over what should be included in the Commissioner's return to the Court. At pp. 347-351, his Lordship said: Two points can be drawn from these decisions. First, “the matter” to be touched upon is the decision itself or the hearing that led to the decision. Only what was before the decision-maker at the hearing forms the return. Second, there must be a basis or reason for including a paper or document in the record. I will examine each of these propositions. 1. — What is “the matter” being touched upon? What is in issue? “The matter” is determined by what has been put in issue by the originating notice. In many instances what is in issue will be the ultimate decision made by a decision-maker. However, in some judicial reviews the substantive decisions are not the only focus of an attack; challenges can be made to procedural choices and prior, related decisions. To the extent that Broda and Robertson seem to have limited “the matter” to the ultimate decision, I disagree with that conclusion. . . . . . Support for the conclusion that “the matter” is to be determined by what an applicant has put into issue is found in Ady v. Law Society of Alberta (1994), 29 Admin. L.R. (2d) 56 (Alta. C.A.). In Ady the issue was whether the return should have included material relating to decisions made at a lower level of a chain of decision-makers. This court held that as Ady's originating motion addressed the decision of the Hearing Committee but did not request a review of the initial decision of the Conduct Committee, he was barred from “extending through the back door” any additional records relating to the prior, included decision of the Conduct Committee. At paras. 4 and 11-12 the panel stated: We note that the originating motion before the Queen's Bench asks for statutory review of the decision of the Hearing Committee to discipline Mr. Ady. It does not seek statutory review of earlier decisions by the deputy secretary or the Conduct Committee, decisions that may or may not have led to the hearing before the Hearing Committee … Mr. Ady argues that the real object of his original application was the Law Society itself, not the decision of the Hearing Committee, and that the entire matter is all one proceeding. We do not agree. His motion does not say that and, even if it did, we would be inclined to require a more specific attack. These statements suggest that had the earlier decision of the Conduct Committee been placed in issue by Ady, the return may have had to include the papers or documents required to deal with that issue. … The threshold for allegations of differential treatment Administrative decision-makers are to be granted limited deliberative secrecy: Tremblay v. Commission des affaires sociales et autre, [1992] 1 S.C.R. 952, 136 N.R. 5, 47 Q.A.C. 169. The ability to draw conclusions untrammelled by any concern of subsequent disclosure of the thought process and the ability to change those thoughts after further reflection without fear of subsequent criticism or explanation are necessary elements to decision-making: Glengarry Memorial Hospital v. Pay Equity Hearings Tribunal (Ont.) et al. (1993), 60 O.A.C. 161, 99 D.L.R. (4th) 682 (Div. Ct.); leave to appeal denied on this issue (1993), 99 D.L.R. (4th) 706 (Ont. Div. Ct.); see also Ron Ellis and Paul Atterma, Deliberative Secrecy and Adjudicative Independence: The Glengarry Precipice, (1994) 7 C.J.A.L.P. 171. These principles are relevant to an examination of the investigative decision. Deliberative secrecy is not absolute; it must be balanced with deliberative openness. To ensure that a balance is kept, simple allegations or speculation of differential treatment or unfairness are insufficient; a threshold must be met. Such a threshold must include a factual foundation for the allegation in the originating motion. Support for the use of a threshold exists in the British Columbia Court of Appeal decisions of Kuntz v. College of Physicians and Surgeons (B.C.) (1996), 73 B.C.A.C. 167, 120 W.A.C. 167, 21 B.C.L.R. (3d) 219 (C.A.) and Hammami v. College of Physicians and Surgeons (B.C.) (1996), 73 B.C.A.C. 205, 120 W.A.C. 205, 21 B.C.L.R. (3d) 267 (C.A.). In these companion cases, the court held that for a further, more comprehensive production of records for judicial review, there must be an evidentiary basis and the allegations must not be intended to “investigate the possibility”. Similarly, in Tremblay at p. 966 [S.C.R.], the Supreme Court also established a threshold for piercing the veil of deliberative secrecy: by the very nature of the control exercised over their decisions administrative tribunals cannot rely on deliberative secrecy to the same extent as judicial tribunals. Of course, secrecy remains the rule, but it may nonetheless be lifted when the litigant can present valid reasons for believing that the process followed did not comply with the rules of natural justice. In Waverley (Village Commissioners) et al. v. Kerr et al. (1994), 129 N.S.R. (2d) 298, 362 A.P.R. 298, the Nova Scotia Court of Appeal used similar wording to establish a threshold: A distinction exists between discovery, which is a somewhat unfocussed fact gathering exercise, and the examination of witnesses in the course of a judicial review, when issues are more defined and questions must be relevant to them. In either case, discovery or testimony, a proper evidentiary foundation must be created, generally by affidavit evidence, to establish that valid reasons exist for concern that there has been a want of natural justice or procedural fairness, or that the discretionary authority has been otherwise exceeded. Thus a party must show that there is a valid reason for belief in the allegation before records related to that matter must be included in the return. A valid reason for belief can be shown by affidavit. Another way in which a valid reason for belief is established is through the actions or admissions of a decision-maker. … 2. — What does “touching” the matter mean? What constitutes something which “touches” the matter? I conclude that the items which “touch” the matter are broader than the items specifically enumerated in rule 753.13(1)(a)(b) and (c). If rule 753.13(1)(d) were limited to the items specifically enumerated, the use of the term “touching the matter” would be unnecessary. The phrase “touching the matter” was originally included in rule 200(1) which allowed parties at examination for discovery to examine other parties on anything “touching the matters in question”. On November 1, 1999 this phrase was replaced with the test of relevance and materiality. In this context, there is substantial case law giving the phrase a broad and expansive meaning. In Canadian Utilities Ltd. v. Mannix Ltd. et al. (1959), 27 W.W.R. (N.S.) 508 (Alta. T.D.), at p. 521, Riley, J., held that the discovery rules permitted greater latitude than that permitted by the rules of admissibility at trial. The term “touching the matters in question” was found to be broader in scope than “material” and “relevant”. Justice Haddad took a similar approach in Czuy v. Mitchell et al. (1976), 1 A.R. 434, 72 D.L.R. (3d) 424 (C.A.), at p. 427-429. He concluded that questions which were relevant to the matters in issue or which could possibly affect the issues between the parties, were questions which touched the matters in question. Prior to 1977, British Columbia's discovery rules also contained the phrase “touching the matters in question.” Again, the phrase was broadly interpreted. Relevant questions, and even potentially relevant questions, touch the matters in question: see Hopper v. Dunsmuir (1903), 10 B.C.R. 23 (C.A.); Wismer v. Maclean-Hunter Publishing Co. and Fraser No. 2 (1953), 10 W.W.R.(N.S.) 625 (B.C.C.A.); Cominco Ltd. v. Westinghouse Canada Ltd. (1979), 11 B.C.L.R. 142 (C.A.). Other courts have also broadly interpreted similar phrases. In Saskatchewan, rule 222 permits oral discovery “touching the matters in issue in the action”. The interpretation of this phrase is consistent with that in British Columbia and Alberta. Something less than materiality or relevance is required: see R. and Minister of Highways v. Wells (W.C.) Construction Co. (1969), 72 W.W.R.(N.S.) 121 (Sask. Q.B.); Cominco Ltd. v. Phillips Cables Ltd. et al., [1987] 3 W.W.R. 562, 54 Sask.R. 134 (C.A.); Steier et al. v. University Hospital Board et al., [1988] 4 W.W.R. 303, 67 Sask. R. 81 (C.A.). In Compagnie Financière et Commerciale du Pacifique v. Peruvian Guano Co. (1882), 11 Q.B.D. 55 (C.A.), the English Court of Appeal interpreted the phrase “relating to any matter in question” in Order XXXI rule 12. The court held at p. 62-65 that the phrase included documents: … which not only would be evidence upon any issue, but also which, it is reasonable to suppose, contains information which may—not which must—either directly or indirectly enable the party requiring the affidavit to advance his own case, or to damage the case of his adversary … a document can properly be said to contain information which may enable the party requiring the affidavit to either advance his own case or to damage the case of his adversary, if it is a document which may fairly lead him to a train of inquiry… These interpretations provide some guidance. Concerns about far ranging returns are alleviated by the fact that the return is only directed at what is in issue. Moreover, in circumstances where the administrative decision-maker is insulated from investigative and other preliminary processes, the decision-maker will not possess documents relating to those functions and cannot be expected to include them in the return. Demands for more expansive returns cannot become fishing expeditions because the party attacking administrative decisions will not be granted access to the documents unless they have raised a valid reason for belief in the allegations underlying their attack. The Commissioner is required to include in his return all things which touch on the issue of his decision to conduct an investigation and to issue an order relating only to the disclosures made by pharmacists and pharmacies to IMS. 2. Transcript or Recording Must Be Forwarded The words of Rule 753.13(1) are quite broad and equally clear: “the judgment, order or decision, as the case may be, together with the process commencing the proceedings, the evidence and all exhibits filed, if any, and all things touching the matter and the notice served on him…” This is sufficiently broad to include the transcript and any evidence considered by the tribunal. If a transcript is not available, but the proceedings were mechanically or otherwise recorded, submission of such records would be sufficient to comply with the Rules. Friends of the Old Man River Society v. Assn. of Professional Engineers, Geologists & Geophysicists (Alberta) (1997), 55 Alta. L.R. (3d) 373 (Q.B.), at p. 406, per Cooke J. 3. The Meaning of “All other papers …” In Robertson v. Edmonton (City) Police Service, 2004 ABQB 243, 2004 CarswellAlta 511, 355 A.R. 281, 39 Alta. L.R. (4th) 239, Slatter J. said, at p. 298: The requirement to produce “all other papers or documents touching the matter” does not mean that the tribunal has to make full disclosure of all records in its possession or power. For the purposes of the Return the “matter” is the decision and the way it was made. Generally only documents that were actually before the decision-maker at the time the decision was made need be included: Broda v. Edmonton (City), supra, at paras. 6-12; Labour Relations Board (Alta.) v. International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers, Local 1007 (1991), 83 Alta. L.R. (2d) 253, § 18 (Q.B.); Ady v. Law Society of Alberta (1994), 29 Admin. L.R. (2d) 56, (C.A.). 4. No Right of Examination except under the Rules In Operative Plasterers' and Cement Masons' International Association of the United States and Canada, Local 222 v. Alberta, 2007 ABQB 34, 2007 CarswellAlta 77, 413 A.R. 184, Bielby J. said, at p. 187: In the absence of a Rule of Court or other statutory authority authorizing same, the Applicants are not entitled to conduct an examination as if for discovery of the party who certified the contents of a Return filed in relation to an application for judicial review. Her Ladyship then said, at pp. 191-192: There is no requirement in the Rules of Court nor elsewhere that the Crown submit to an examination or cross-examination on the contents of a Return. The subject of the contents of the Return may be canvassed during the course of a Rule 266 examination, however.

Information and Privacy Commissioner, 2005 ABCA 325, 2005 CarswellAlta 1416, 376 A.R.
L.R.
(4th) 201, Ritter J.A. discussed what must be returned under Rule 753.13.
In that case, the Alberta Information and Privacy Commissioner had decided to investigate certain disclosures made by pharmacies to IMS Health Canada Ltd.
(a company that collected and analyzed information concerning health care).
IMS sought judicial review of the Commissioner's decision, and a dispute arose over what should be included in the Commissioner's return to the Court.
At pp.
347-351, his Lordship said: Two points can be drawn from these decisions.
First, “the matter” to be touched upon is the decision itself or the hearing that led to the decision.
Only what was before the decision-maker at the hearing forms the return.
Second, there must be a basis or reason for including a paper or document in the record.
I will examine each of these propositions.
1. — What is “the matter” being touched upon?
What is in issue? “The matter” is determined by what has been put in issue by the originating notice.
In many instances what is in issue will be the ultimate decision made by a decision-maker.
However, in some judicial reviews the substantive decisions are not the only focus of an attack; challenges can be made to procedural choices and prior, related decisions.
To the extent that Broda and Robertson seem to have limited “the matter” to the ultimate decision, I disagree with that conclusion. . . . . .
Support for the conclusion that “the matter” is to be determined by what an applicant has put into issue is found in Ady v.
Law Society of Alberta (1994), 29 Admin.
L.R.
(2d) 56 (Alta.
In Ady the issue was whether the return should have included material relating to decisions made at a lower level of a chain of decision-makers.

This court held that as Ady's originating motion addressed the decision of the Hearing Committee but did not request a review of the initial decision of the Conduct Committee, he was barred from “extending through the back door” any additional records relating to the prior, included decision of the Conduct Committee.
At paras.
4 and 11-12 the panel stated: We note that the originating motion before the Queen's Bench asks for statutory review of the decision of the Hearing Committee to discipline Mr.
Ady.
It does not seek statutory review of earlier decisions by the deputy secretary or the Conduct Committee, decisions that may or may not have led to the hearing before the Hearing Committee … Mr.
Ady argues that the real object of his original application was the Law Society itself, not the decision of the Hearing Committee, and that the entire matter is all one proceeding.
We do not agree.
His motion does not say that and, even if it did, we would be inclined to require a more specific attack.

These statements suggest that had the earlier decision of the Conduct Committee been placed in issue by Ady, the return may have had to include the papers or documents required to deal with that issue. … The threshold for allegations of differential treatment Administrative decision-makers are to be granted limited deliberative secrecy: Tremblay v.
Commission des affaires sociales et autre, [1992] 1 S.C.R.

The ability to draw conclusions untrammelled by any concern of subsequent disclosure of the thought process and the ability to change those thoughts after further reflection without fear of subsequent criticism or explanation are necessary elements to decision-making: Glengarry Memorial Hospital v.
Pay Equity Hearings Tribunal (Ont.) et al.
Ct.); leave to appeal denied on this issue (1993), 99 D.L.R.
Div.
Ct.); see also Ron Ellis and Paul Atterma, Deliberative Secrecy and Adjudicative Independence: The Glengarry Precipice, (1994) 7 C.J.A.L.P.
These principles are relevant to an examination of the investigative decision.
Deliberative secrecy is not absolute; it must be balanced with deliberative openness.
To ensure that a balance is kept, simple allegations or speculation of differential treatment or unfairness are insufficient; a threshold must be met.
Such a threshold must include a factual foundation for the allegation in the originating motion.
Support for the use of a threshold exists in the British Columbia Court of Appeal decisions of Kuntz v.
College of Physicians and Surgeons (B.C.) (1996), 73 B.C.A.C.
(3d) 219 (C.A.) and Hammami v.
College of Physicians and Surgeons (B.C.) (1996), 73 B.C.A.C.

In these companion cases, the court held that for a further, more comprehensive production of records for judicial review, there must be an evidentiary basis and the allegations must not be intended to “investigate the possibility”.
Similarly, in Tremblay at p.

966 [S.C.R.], the Supreme Court also established a threshold for piercing the veil of deliberative secrecy: by the very nature of the control exercised over their decisions administrative tribunals cannot rely on deliberative secrecy to the same extent as judicial tribunals.

Of course, secrecy remains the rule, but it may nonetheless be lifted when the litigant can present valid reasons for believing that the process followed did not comply with the rules of natural justice.
In Waverley (Village Commissioners) et al. v.
Kerr et al.

298, the Nova Scotia Court of Appeal used similar wording to establish a threshold: A distinction exists between discovery, which is a somewhat unfocussed fact gathering exercise, and the examination of witnesses in the course of a judicial review, when issues are more defined and questions must be relevant to them.

In either case, discovery or testimony, a proper evidentiary foundation must be created, generally by affidavit evidence, to establish that valid reasons exist for concern that there has been a want of natural justice or procedural fairness, or that the discretionary authority has been otherwise exceeded.
Thus a party must show that there is a valid reason for belief in the allegation before records related to that matter must be included in the return.
A valid reason for belief can be shown by affidavit.
Another way in which a valid reason for belief is established is through the actions or admissions of a decision-maker. … 2. — What does “touching” the matter mean?
What constitutes something which “touches” the matter?
I conclude that the items which “touch” the matter are broader than the items specifically enumerated in rule 753.13(1)(a)(b) and (c).
If rule 753.13(1)(d) were limited to the items specifically enumerated, the use of the term “touching the matter” would be unnecessary.
The phrase “touching the matter” was originally included in rule 200(1) which allowed parties at examination for discovery to examine other parties on anything “touching the matters in question”.
On November 1, 1999 this phrase was replaced with the test of relevance and materiality.
In this context, there is substantial case law giving the phrase a broad and expansive meaning.
In Canadian Utilities Ltd. v.
Mannix Ltd. et al.
(N.S.) 508 (Alta.
T.D.), at p.
521, Riley, J., held that the discovery rules permitted greater latitude than that permitted by the rules of admissibility at trial.
The term “touching the matters in question” was found to be broader in scope than “material” and “relevant”.
Justice Haddad took a similar approach in Czuy v.
Mitchell et al.
He concluded that questions which were relevant to the matters in issue or which could possibly affect the issues between the parties, were questions which touched the matters in question.
Prior to 1977, British Columbia's discovery rules also contained the phrase “touching the matters in question.” Again, the phrase was broadly interpreted.
Relevant questions, and even potentially relevant questions, touch the matters in question: see Hopper v.
Dunsmuir (1903), 10 B.C.R.
23 (C.A.); Wismer v.
Maclean-Hunter Publishing Co. and Fraser No.
2 (1953), 10 W.W.R.(N.S.) 625 (B.C.C.A.); Cominco Ltd. v.
Westinghouse Canada Ltd.
Other courts have also broadly interpreted similar phrases.
In Saskatchewan, rule 222 permits oral discovery “touching the matters in issue in the action”.
The interpretation of this phrase is consistent with that in British Columbia and Alberta.
Something less than materiality or relevance is required: see R. and Minister of Highways v.
Wells (W.C.) Construction Co.
Q.B.); Cominco Ltd. v.
Phillips Cables Ltd. et al., [1987] 3 W.W.R.
134 (C.A.); Steier et al. v.
University Hospital Board et al., [1988] 4 W.W.R.
R.
In Compagnie Financière et Commerciale du Pacifique v.
Peruvian Guano Co.
55 (C.A.), the English Court of Appeal interpreted the phrase “relating to any matter in question” in Order XXXI rule 12.
The court held at p.

62-65 that the phrase included documents: … which not only would be evidence upon any issue, but also which, it is reasonable to suppose, contains information which may—not which must—either directly or indirectly enable the party requiring the affidavit to advance his own case, or to damage the case of his adversary … a document can properly be said to contain information which may enable the party requiring the affidavit to either advance his own case or to damage the case of his adversary, if it is a document which may fairly lead him to a train of inquiry… These interpretations provide some guidance.
Concerns about far ranging returns are alleviated by the fact that the return is only directed at what is in issue.

Moreover, in circumstances where the administrative decision-maker is insulated from investigative and other preliminary processes, the decision-maker will not possess documents relating to those functions and cannot be expected to include them in the return.

Demands for more expansive returns cannot become fishing expeditions because the party attacking administrative decisions will not be granted access to the documents unless they have raised a valid reason for belief in the allegations underlying their attack.

The Commissioner is required to include in his return all things which touch on the issue of his decision to conduct an investigation and to issue an order relating only to the disclosures made by pharmacists and pharmacies to IMS.

Transcript or Recording Must Be Forwarded The words of Rule 753.13(1) are quite broad and equally clear: “the judgment, order or decision, as the case may be, together with the process commencing the proceedings, the evidence and all exhibits filed, if any, and all things touching the matter and the notice served on him…” This is sufficiently broad to include the transcript and any evidence considered by the tribunal.
If a transcript is not available, but the proceedings were mechanically or otherwise recorded, submission of such records would be sufficient to comply with the Rules.
Friends of the Old Man River Society v.
Assn. of Professional Engineers, Geologists & Geophysicists (Alberta) (1997), 55 Alta.
L.R.
406, per Cooke J.
The Meaning of “All other papers …” In Robertson v.
Edmonton (City) Police Service, 2004 ABQB 243, 2004 CarswellAlta 511, 355 A.R.
L.R.
(4th) 239, Slatter J. said, at p.
298: The requirement to produce “all other papers or documents touching the matter” does not mean that the tribunal has to make full disclosure of all records in its possession or power.
For the purposes of the Return the “matter” is the decision and the way it was made.
Generally only documents that were actually before the decision-maker at the time the decision was made need be included: Broda v.
Edmonton (City), supra, at paras.
6-12; Labour Relations Board (Alta.) v.
International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers, Local 1007 (1991), 83 Alta.
L.R.
Law Society of Alberta (1994), 29 Admin.
L.R.
No Right of Examination except under the Rules In Operative Plasterers' and Cement Masons' International Association of the United States and Canada, Local 222 v.
Alberta, 2007 ABQB 34, 2007 CarswellAlta 77, 413 A.R.
184, Bielby J. said, at p.

187: In the absence of a Rule of Court or other statutory authority authorizing same, the Applicants are not entitled to conduct an examination as if for discovery of the party who certified the contents of a Return filed in relation to an application for judicial review.
Her Ladyship then said, at pp.
191-192: There is no requirement in the Rules of Court nor elsewhere that the Crown submit to an examination or cross-examination on the contents of a Return.
The subject of the contents of the Return may be canvassed during the course of a Rule 266 examination, however.

sentences.text: Other circumstances when record of proceedings may be required

paragraphs.text: (1) The Court may make an order for the production of the certified record of proceedings of a person or body if the conditions described in subrule (2) are met. (2) The conditions are: (a) the originating application for judicial review is for an order other than an order to set aside a decision or act; (b) the certified record of proceedings is required to establish the claim; (c) the person or body that is the subject of the originating application has not sent to the court clerk the certified record of proceedings within a reasonable time after the originating applicant's written request for the person or body to do so. (3) If the Court orders the certified record of proceedings to be sent to the court clerk, rules 3.18(3) and 3.19 apply, unless the Court otherwise orders.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 3.22:1 Rule 3.22 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.22. 1. New Evidence In University of Alberta v. Alberta (Information & Privacy Commissioner), 2011 ABQB 699, 2011 CarswellAlta 2050, 525 A.R. 58, Lee, J. discussed the topic of putting new evidence before a court conducting a judicial review. At paragraphs 14–23, his Lordship said: 14 Finally, Alberta jurisprudence has clearly set out a more restrictive approach to admitting new documents and evidence in a judicial review. Alberta case law clearly establishes that additional evidence is only admissible in judicial review in limited situations. Slatter J, as he then was, noted in Alberta Liquor Store Assn v. Alberta (Gaming and Liquor Commission), 2006 ABQB 904 at para. 40: The general rule is that judicial review is conducted based on the Return filed by the tribunal. Neither Rule 406 nor Rule 753.08 require an affidavit in support. The record before the tribunal is generally the record before the Court, and additional affidavits and evidence are exceptional: White v. Alberta (Workers' Compensation Board Appeals Commission), 2006 ABQB 359, 57 Alta. L.R. (4th) 282, 41 Admin. L.R. (4th) 141, at para. 35. 15 Slatter J then went on to note the limited instances where supplementary evidence may be allowed: a. to show bias, or a reasonable apprehension of bias, if the facts in support of the allegation do not appear on the record. b. to demonstrate a breach of the rules of natural justice not apparent from the record, c. to address issues like standing; d. where the tribunal makes no, or an inadequate, record of its proceedings, affidavits are permissible to show what evidence was actually placed before the tribunal; (sic) 16 Slatter J. then quoted S. Blake in Administrative Law in Canada, (4th ed.), at pg. 198: Only material that was considered by the tribunal in coming to its decision is relevant on judicial review. It is not the role of the court to decide the matter anew. The court simply conducts a review of the tribunal decision. For this reason, the only evidence that is admissible before the court is the record that was before the tribunal. Evidence that was not before the tribunal is not admissible without leave of the court. If the issue to be decided on the application involves a question of law, or concerns the tribunal's statutory authority, the court will refuse leave to file additional evidence. Evidence challenging the wisdom of the decision is not admissible. The tribunal's findings of fact may not be challenged with evidence that was not put before the tribunal. Fresh evidence, discovered since the tribunal made its decision, is not admissible on judicial review. … (footnotes omitted). (Emphasis added) 17 Slatter J concluded (at para. 42) that: Attempting to introduce fresh evidence respecting the merits of the challenged decision on an application for judicial review misapprehends the nature of judicial review. 18 This general rule is necessary given the nature of judicial review. In judicial review, the tribunal's decision is not subject to appeal, but to a determination of whether the decision meets the requisite standard of review. The judge on review is looking at the tribunal's reasons to determine whether, based on the evidence before the tribunal, it reached a rational decision (reasonableness standard) or a correct decision (correctness standard). Slatter J addressed this point (at para. 43):— Whatever the standard of review, the review must be conducted on the record that the tribunal had … Whether there is a rational basis for the decision can only be determined by examining the evidence the tribunal had to work with: Western Canada Wilderness Committee v. British Columbia (Ministry of Forests, South Island Forest District)[2002] B.C.J. No. 2036, supra, at paras. 32-33; Alberta Union of Provincial Employees v. Alberta (Provincial Health Authorities), [2006] A.J. No. 1480, 2006 ABCA 356, at para. 18; Memorial University of Newfoundland v. Canadian Union of Public Employees, Local 1615 (2000), 194 Nfld. & P.E.I.R. 190, at para. 9, 29 Admin. L.R. (3d) 100 at para. 63; CAIMAW, Local 14 v. Paccar of Canada Ltd., [1989] 2 S.C.R. 983, at para. 43 (Sopinka J. concurring.) … Whether a decision is reasonable is not a search for some sort of universal truth: Ryan, [2003] 1 S.C.R. 247, supra, at para. 51. Any tribunal or court can only work with the evidence before it, and a decision may well prove to be reasonable, even though it can arguably be shown to be factually flawed. It follows that new evidence relating to the merits of the decision will seldom be admissible, as it is irrelevant to the issues before the court on judicial review. (Emphasis added) 19 Slatter J also rejected the submission that the test for new evidence in judicial review was that set out in R v. Palmer, [1980] 1 SCR 759. Palmer concerned fresh evidence in an appeal. He noted (at para. 44):— … the analogy between the two types of proceedings [judicial review and appeal] is inapt. When an application for judicial review is brought, all of the evidence is “fresh”, in the sense that there is no evidence on the record of the Court prior to the commencement of the application, and there is no prior record to “refresh”… It, however, confuses the entire concept of judicial review to suggest that evidence that was not before the tribunal can be brought forward on judicial review simply because it is “fresh” within the Palmer rule. Such evidence can never be “decisive” of the application, because the issues are different. The Board had to decide whether to grant a retail liquor license. The Court has to decide whether the granting of the license meets the appropriate standard of review, and complies with the rules of natural justice. The Court does not decide whether the license should have been granted, and it is not helpful to say that the new evidence will be “decisive” in this context. On the other hand, evidence might be admitted on judicial review even if it is not “decisive” of anything previously decided. For example, if subsequently obtained evidence shows a reasonable apprehension of bias, it might well be admitted on judicial review. Such evidence is not decisive of any issue that the Board has previously decided, but it is a valid ground for judicial review. I therefore conclude (contrary to my earlier assumption in White v. Alberta (Workers' Compensation Board), supra, at para. 34) that the Palmer test for fresh evidence on appeal has no application in this context. 20 Similarly here, the Court is not to decide whether documents sought were within the custody and control of the University of Alberta; the Court's role is to determine whether the Adjudicator's decision met the requisite standard of review and complies with the principles of natural justice and the duty to be fair. 21 Perhaps most importantly, Slatter J noted (at para. 46):— Whenever it may be appropriate to file affidavits on judicial review applications one thing is clear: the applicants are not entitled to turn the judicial review application in a trial de novo on the merits of the issue before the tribunal. Here, the Applicants are entitled to show that the Board was incorrect, unreasonable, or patently unreasonable, depending on the ultimate standard of review that is selected. They are not however entitled to ask the Court to usurp the jurisdiction of the Board, and decide de novo … (Emphasis added) 22 These issues were also considered in Dodd v. Alberta (Registrar of Motor Vehicle Services), 2010 ABQB 184 where the Court noted at paras. 16 -17:— The relevance of evidence on a judicial review application depends on the grounds for review that have been alleged: Dechant v. Law Society of Alberta, [2000] A.J. No. 1163, at para. 17. For example, where the grounds are bias or reasonable apprehension of bias, or breach of natural justice, the relevant circumstances may not appear on the record and evidence relating to these issues will be admitted … Evidence is also admissible on a judicial review application where the record of proceedings is inadequate, in which case evidence may be admitted to “show what evidence was actually placed before the tribunal”… 23 See also 979899 Alberta Ltd. v. Alberta, 2008 ABQB 57 at para. 5; 1254582 Alberta Ltd. (c.o.b. Airport Taxi Service) v. Miscellaneous Employees Teamsters, Local Union 987 of Alberta, 2009 ABQB 127 at paras. 26 and 27; McClary v. Geophysical Services Inc., 2011 ABQB 112 at paras. 23 to 26; O'Malley v. Calgary Separate School District No. 1, 2006 ABQB 126 at para. 9; and Czerwinski v. Mulaner, 2007 ABQB 536 at paras. 21 and 22. In Caron v. Alberta (Human Rights Commission, Chief Commissioner), 2013 ABQB 13, 2013 CarswellAlta 2955, 551 A.R. 355, Madam Justice Moreau, in referring to Rule 3.22, said, at paragraphs 24–26: 24 Slatter J. (as he then was) discussed the equivalent rule in Alberta Liquor Store Assn v. Alberta (Gaming and Liquor Commission), 2006 ABQB 904, 406 AR 104, paras 40 to 42. He concluded that a reviewing court is bound by the record which was before the tribunal whose decision is being reviewed. The admission of new evidence on a judicial review is exceptional, for example, to demonstrate bias. See also Sarg Oils Ltd v. (Alberta) Environmental Appeal Board, 2007 ABCA 215, 75 Admin LR (4th) 314, para 15; Silverman v. Alberta (Human Rights Commission), 2012 ABQB 152, paras 9 to 14. 25 Slatter J. commented in Alberta Liquor Stores: 46 Whenever it may be appropriate to file affidavits on judicial review applications one thing is clear: the applicants are not entitled to turn the judicial review application[into] a trial de novo on the merits of the issue before the tribunal … 26 In other words, the main purpose of judicial review is to review a decision, not to replace the decision with that of the reviewing court. See also Bauhuis v. Association of Professional Engineers and Geoscientists, 2024 ABKB 603 at paragraphs 24-25. 2. When is permission required? In Dr. Mays Abdulghafoor v. University of Calgary, 2021 ABQB 187, 2021 CarswellAlta 617, Justice Jeffrey said: [63] The wording of Rule 3.22(d) says the court's permission is required before questioning, if a transcript of such questioning is intended to be used at the judicial review hearing (“no one may be questioned … without the Court's permission”). Under Rule 3.22, however, the Court's permission is only required before the Court considers the additional evidence; it does not appear that the permission must precede the preparation, swearing, filing, service or even a party's reliance upon the evidence, only before the Court considers it. Prudent practice would dictate, of course, a party request the Court's permission before relying on the added evidence, since reliance suggests they commend it to the Court for its consideration. … [65] Rule 3.22(d) provides the Court broad discretion to permit supplementary evidence on judicial review. When the merits of a decision are challenged, the reviewing Court considers just the information before the decision maker; when the challenge is to the process followed by the decision maker, it may be necessary to permit additional evidence: Bergman v Innisfree (Village), 2020 ABQB 661 paras 41 to 48. The limited circumstances under which supplementary information may be permitted include (Bergman, at para 45): a) to address standing; b) to show bias or a reasonable apprehension of bias where the facts in support of the allegation do not appear on the record; c) to demonstrate a breach of the rules of natural justice not apparent on the record; d) to reveal the evidence actually placed before the decision maker where the decision maker provided an inadequate or no record of its proceedings.

43 (Sopinka J. concurring.) … Whether a decision is reasonable is not a search for some sort of universal truth: Ryan, [2003] 1 S.C.R.
247, supra, at para.
Any tribunal or court can only work with the evidence before it, and a decision may well prove to be reasonable, even though it can arguably be shown to be factually flawed.
It follows that new evidence relating to the merits of the decision will seldom be admissible, as it is irrelevant to the issues before the court on judicial review.
(Emphasis added) 19 Slatter J also rejected the submission that the test for new evidence in judicial review was that set out in R v.
Palmer, [1980] 1 SCR 759.
Palmer concerned fresh evidence in an appeal.
He noted (at para.
44):— … the analogy between the two types of proceedings [judicial review and appeal] is inapt.

When an application for judicial review is brought, all of the evidence is “fresh”, in the sense that there is no evidence on the record of the Court prior to the commencement of the application, and there is no prior record to “refresh”… It, however, confuses the entire concept of judicial review to suggest that evidence that was not before the tribunal can be brought forward on judicial review simply because it is “fresh” within the Palmer rule.
Such evidence can never be “decisive” of the application, because the issues are different.
The Board had to decide whether to grant a retail liquor license.
The Court has to decide whether the granting of the license meets the appropriate standard of review, and complies with the rules of natural justice.
The Court does not decide whether the license should have been granted, and it is not helpful to say that the new evidence will be “decisive” in this context.
On the other hand, evidence might be admitted on judicial review even if it is not “decisive” of anything previously decided.
For example, if subsequently obtained evidence shows a reasonable apprehension of bias, it might well be admitted on judicial review.
Such evidence is not decisive of any issue that the Board has previously decided, but it is a valid ground for judicial review.
I therefore conclude (contrary to my earlier assumption in White v.
Alberta (Workers' Compensation Board), supra, at para.
34) that the Palmer test for fresh evidence on appeal has no application in this context.

20 Similarly here, the Court is not to decide whether documents sought were within the custody and control of the University of Alberta; the Court's role is to determine whether the Adjudicator's decision met the requisite standard of review and complies with the principles of natural justice and the duty to be fair.
21 Perhaps most importantly, Slatter J noted (at para.

46):— Whenever it may be appropriate to file affidavits on judicial review applications one thing is clear: the applicants are not entitled to turn the judicial review application in a trial de novo on the merits of the issue before the tribunal.
Here, the Applicants are entitled to show that the Board was incorrect, unreasonable, or patently unreasonable, depending on the ultimate standard of review that is selected.
They are not however entitled to ask the Court to usurp the jurisdiction of the Board, and decide de novo … (Emphasis added) 22 These issues were also considered in Dodd v.
Alberta (Registrar of Motor Vehicle Services), 2010 ABQB 184 where the Court noted at paras.
16 -17:— The relevance of evidence on a judicial review application depends on the grounds for review that have been alleged: Dechant v.
Law Society of Alberta, [2000] A.J.
No.
1163, at para.

For example, where the grounds are bias or reasonable apprehension of bias, or breach of natural justice, the relevant circumstances may not appear on the record and evidence relating to these issues will be admitted … Evidence is also admissible on a judicial review application where the record of proceedings is inadequate, in which case evidence may be admitted to “show what evidence was actually placed before the tribunal”… 23 See also 979899 Alberta Ltd. v.
Alberta, 2008 ABQB 57 at para.
5; 1254582 Alberta Ltd.
(c.o.b.
Airport Taxi Service) v.
Miscellaneous Employees Teamsters, Local Union 987 of Alberta, 2009 ABQB 127 at paras.
26 and 27; McClary v.
Geophysical Services Inc., 2011 ABQB 112 at paras.
23 to 26; O'Malley v.
Calgary Separate School District No.
1, 2006 ABQB 126 at para.
9; and Czerwinski v.
Mulaner, 2007 ABQB 536 at paras.
In Caron v.
Alberta (Human Rights Commission, Chief Commissioner), 2013 ABQB 13, 2013 CarswellAlta 2955, 551 A.R.
355, Madam Justice Moreau, in referring to Rule 3.22, said, at paragraphs 24–26: 24 Slatter J.
(as he then was) discussed the equivalent rule in Alberta Liquor Store Assn v.
Alberta (Gaming and Liquor Commission), 2006 ABQB 904, 406 AR 104, paras 40 to 42.
He concluded that a reviewing court is bound by the record which was before the tribunal whose decision is being reviewed.
The admission of new evidence on a judicial review is exceptional, for example, to demonstrate bias.
See also Sarg Oils Ltd v.
(Alberta) Environmental Appeal Board, 2007 ABCA 215, 75 Admin LR (4th) 314, para 15; Silverman v.
Alberta (Human Rights Commission), 2012 ABQB 152, paras 9 to 14.

25 Slatter J. commented in Alberta Liquor Stores: 46 Whenever it may be appropriate to file affidavits on judicial review applications one thing is clear: the applicants are not entitled to turn the judicial review application[into] a trial de novo on the merits of the issue before the tribunal … 26 In other words, the main purpose of judicial review is to review a decision, not to replace the decision with that of the reviewing court.
See also Bauhuis v.
Association of Professional Engineers and Geoscientists, 2024 ABKB 603 at paragraphs 24-25.
When is permission required?
In Dr.
Mays Abdulghafoor v.

University of Calgary, 2021 ABQB 187, 2021 CarswellAlta 617, Justice Jeffrey said: [63] The wording of Rule 3.22(d) says the court's permission is required before questioning, if a transcript of such questioning is intended to be used at the judicial review hearing (“no one may be questioned … without the Court's permission”).

Under Rule 3.22, however, the Court's permission is only required before the Court considers the additional evidence; it does not appear that the permission must precede the preparation, swearing, filing, service or even a party's reliance upon the evidence, only before the Court considers it.

Prudent practice would dictate, of course, a party request the Court's permission before relying on the added evidence, since reliance suggests they commend it to the Court for its consideration. … [65] Rule 3.22(d) provides the Court broad discretion to permit supplementary evidence on judicial review.

When the merits of a decision are challenged, the reviewing Court considers just the information before the decision maker; when the challenge is to the process followed by the decision maker, it may be necessary to permit additional evidence: Bergman v Innisfree (Village), 2020 ABQB 661 paras 41 to 48.

The limited circumstances under which supplementary information may be permitted include (Bergman, at para 45): a) to address standing; b) to show bias or a reasonable apprehension of bias where the facts in support of the allegation do not appear on the record; c) to demonstrate a breach of the rules of natural justice not apparent on the record; d) to reveal the evidence actually placed before the decision maker where the decision maker provided an inadequate or no record of its proceedings.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 3.23:1 Rule 3.23 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.23. 1. Jurisdiction to grant a stay In Société Culturelle Mamowapik v. Alberta (Gaming & Liquor Commission), 2000 ABCA 148, 2000 CarswellAlta 485, 261 A.R. 198, 83 Alta. L.R. (3d) 266, the applicant had its bingo licence revoked by the Commission. The applicant sought a stay of the Commission's order pending the hearing of a judicial review application. The learned Chambers judge in the Court of Queen's Bench refused to grant a stay. The applicant then sought an order from Russell, J.A., sitting alone, reversing the Chambers decision. In concluding that she did not have jurisdiction, her Ladyship said, at pp. 267-268: The applicants rely on Rule 753.15(1) of the Alberta Rules of Court in seeking relief. Unless otherwise provided by statute, that Rule permits the court hearing the application for judicial review, to stay the operation of the decision sought to be set aside pending final determination of the review. That Rule does not permit a further application de novo before a single judge of this court. This court does not have jurisdiction to stay the Board's decision in judicial review proceedings. Counsel for the applicants properly interpreted paragraph F (5) of the Consolidated Court of Appeal Practice Directions, to permit applications for a stay to be heard by a single judge. But a stay of an order refusing a stay is a hollow remedy. What the applicants really seek is a reversal of the stays, which are tantamount to an appeal of those decisions. Although the refusal of the stay, may be the subject of an appeal to this court, those appeals must be heard by a panel consisting of a quorum of judges. . . . . . The present applications for a stay of a refusal of a stay are similar in that they amount to a rehearing of the interlocutory stay applications or sitting on an appeal of them, neither of which I have jurisdiction to preside over, sitting as a single judge of this Court. 2. Test for a stay under the Rule In Fawcett v. College of Physicians and Surgeons of the Province of Alberta, 2019 ABQB 788, 2019 CarswellAlta 2133, Justice Little said: [7] The parties agree that pursuant to authorities including Johnston v Alberta (Director of Vital Statistics), 2007 ABCA 394 and Sobeys West Inc. v Alberta College of Pharmacists, 2014 ABQB 333, the test for a stay under Rule 3.23 is the same as for an interlocutory injunction as set out in RJR-MacDonald v Canada (Attorney General) and which may be summarized as follows: 1. Whether there is a serious issue to be tried. 2. Whether the applicant would suffer irreparable harm if the application were refused. 3. Whether the balance of convenience favours the applicant. 3. This Rule only addresses staying the operation of the actual order or decision This Rule allows the reviewing Court to enter a stay of the operation of the actual order or decision which is sought to be set aside through the judicial review. The Rule does not address the ability of the Court whose decision is the subject of the judicial review to continue with the proceedings before that Court. That Court's jurisdiction in relation to those proceedings is suspended by operation of law (see the annotation under Rule 3.15: “Service of notice of the application suspends proceedings in the Alberta Court of Justice”).

paragraphs.heading: Part 3. Court Actions

sentences.text: Additional remedies on judicial review

paragraphs.text: (1) If an originating applicant is entitled to a declaration that a decision or act of a person or body is unauthorized or invalid, the Court may, instead of making a declaration, set aside the decision or act. (2) The Court may (a) direct a person or body to reconsider the whole or any part of a matter, (b) direct a person or body to reconsider the whole or any part of a decision if the Court has set aside the decision under subrule (1), and (c) give any other directions it considers necessary. (3) If the sole ground for a remedy is a defect in form or a technical irregularity, the Court may, if the Court finds that no substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice has occurred, despite the defect, (a) refuse a remedy, or (b) validate the decision made to have effect from a date and subject to any terms and conditions that the Court considers appropriate. 1. Overview of Court's Discretion In Morawetz v. Alberta (Director of SafeRoads), 2024 ABKB 588, Justice Marion discussed the Court's discretion to direct an administrative tribunal to reconsider its decision. His Lordship said: [30] Rules 3.24(2)(a) and (b) provide the Court a wide discretion to direct an administrative tribunal to reconsider a whole or part of a matter, or to reconsider whole or part of a decision where the Court quashes the decision. Rule 3.24(c) provides the Court jurisdiction to give any other direction it considers necessary in addition to remitting the matter back to the tribunal for reconsideration: Penn v St Stephen's College, 2024 ABCA 99 at para 65. [31] The Court's findings and directions must be considered by and are binding on the tribunal (unless the law changes subsequent to the directions): Régie des rentes du Québec v Canada Bread Company Ltd, 2013 SCC 46 at para 46; Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v Yansane, 2017 FCA 48 at paras 19, 23, 25; Mohammed v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2022 FC 980 at para 44. [32] The discretion to provide directions to an administrative tribunal is part of the multi-faceted question of the appropriate remedy that engages consideration of the Court's common law and statutory jurisdiction and the “great diversity of elements that may influence” the Court's decision in respect of available remedies: Vavilov at para 139. [33] For example, courts outside the SafeRoads context have confirmed the discretion to direct that a reconsideration: (a) be conducted by a different person or panel: United Nurses of Alberta v Alberta Health Services, 2021 ABCA 194 at para 102. There is no fixed rule but, factors considered include fairness and the appearance of impartiality, practicality, and efficiency, the proper administration of justice, cost-efficient decision making and access to justice: United Nurses at paras 103-104; Edmonton Police Service v Furlong, 2013 ABCA 177 at para 3; Vavilov at paras 139-140; (b) be bound by the previous findings of the tribunal: Shuchuk v Alberta (Workers' Compensation Board), 2012 ABCA 50 at para 43 [Shuchuk 2012]. In Sharif v Canada (Attorney General), 2018 FCA 205, at para 54, the Court implied that the tribunal would be bound by its earlier factual findings when the Court decided not to remit the matter due to the inevitable result based on those findings; (c) be limited to specific issues, excluding specific issues, or directing that specifically identified issues must be addressed: Shuchuk 2012 at para 43; Shell Canada Limited v Alberta (Energy), 2023 ABCA 230 at para 59; Yatar v TD Insurance Meloche Monnex, 2024 SCC 8 at para 77; Shuchuk v Alberta (Workers' Compensation Board), 2007 ABCA 213 at para 50; Clark v City of Medicine Hat, 2024 ABKB 513 at paras 71-72; Hannora (Re), 2020 ONCA 161 at para 3; Dr Mays Abdulghafoor v University of Calgary, 2021 ABQB 187 at para 124; Pincher Creek (Town of) v Municipal Government Board, 2006 ABQB 513 at para 18; Shields v Information and Privacy Commissioner, 2004 ABQB 353 at para 74; Schroder v Alberta (Workers' Compensation Board), 2009 ABQB 583 at para 22; Thornhill v Superintendent of Motor Vehicles, 2016 BCSC 1202 at paras 30-31[1]; Kessler v British Columbia (Superintendent of Motor Vehicles), 2017 BCSC 809 at para 20; David Burr Ltd v Zahm, 2012 BCSC 897 at paras 10-13; (d) be based on the original record, or permitting or directing a different or augmented record: Chartrand v Alberta (Human Rights and Citizenship Commission), 2008 ABQB 207 at para 28; Hamilton v Alberta (Labour Relations Board), 1993 CanLII 7143 (AB KB) at para 32; Garnett v British Columbia (Superintendent of Motor Vehicles), 2015 BCSC 1395 at paras 66-67; Byron v British Columbia (Superintendent of Motor Vehicles), 2017 BCSC 1125 at para 81; Cheung v Moorley, 2011 BCSC 1641 at para 77; Alsilmi (Re), 2010 BCSC 282 at para 32-33; Turner v Canada (Attorney General), 2022 FCA 192 at para 9. In Gehl v Canada (Attorney General), 2017 ONCA 319 at para 88, the Court implied the same record would be used in a new hearing when the Court decided that it would be pointless to remit the matter since there was only one possible outcome; and (e) be based on other specific directions of the Court: Shuchuk 2012 at para 42; Dr Mays Abdulghafoor v University of Calgary, 2021 ABQB 187 at paras 121-122; Al-Naami v College of Physicians and Surgeons of Alberta, 2021 ABQB 549 at para 212; Northern Inter-Tribal Health Authority Inc v Yang, 2023 FCA 47 at paras 85-86; Chenjelani v Institute of Chartered Professional Accountants of Saskatchewan, 2022 SKCA 66 at para 55; Chevron Canada Resources v Alberta (Minister of Energy), 1998 ABQB 504 at para 44; Great Canadian Casinos Inc v City of Surrey et al, 2000 BCSC 664 at para 21; Brandt Tractor Ltd v Claypool, 2015 BCSC 759 at para 47; Cheung at para 77; Sunshine Coast Conservation Assn v Sunshine Coast Forest District, 2002 BCSC 145 at para 25. [34] The legislature's ability to limit the Court's remedial powers must be carefully considered in the context of judicial review and its constitutionally enshrined role. See, for example, Dunsmuir v New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9 at para 31. As pointed out in a different context in Smit v Alberta (Director of SafeRoads), 2023 ABKB 435at para 175, it has long been recognized that “the jurisdiction of the superior courts is not taken away, except by express words or necessary implication”, citing: Albon v Pyke (1842), 4 Man & G 421; Canada (Attorney General) v Telezone Inc, 2010 SCC 62 at paras 42-43.
